The Atacama Desert is a desert plateau in South America, mainly in northern Chile, with parts reaching into southern Peru. It is often described as the driest non-polar desert in the world. Some weather stations in its interior have gone many years without recording significant rainfall. The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean on the west and the Andes Mountains on the east, forming a narrow strip that runs north to south along the Pacific coast.

The Atacama covers about 105,000 square kilometres, or roughly 41,000 square miles, though some definitions include nearby arid land as well. Its extreme dryness comes from several factors. The cold Humboldt Current offshore reduces evaporation and cloud formation, the subtropical high-pressure system limits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air from the Amazon Basin. Because of this, much of the region gets only a few millimetres of rain each year, and some central areas can go decades without measurable precipitation.

Even in these conditions, the Atacama supports specialized life. Vegetation is sparse in the most arid parts, but cacti, shrubs, and hardy grasses grow in less extreme areas. Coastal fog, known locally as camanchaca, provides enough moisture to support some ecosystems. The desert is home to insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to dry conditions, while high-altitude wetlands and salt flats support flamingos and other Andean species.

Indigenous peoples have lived in the desert for a long time, including the Atacameño, or Likan Antai, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. Under European colonization, the region came under Spanish rule. In the 19th century, the Atacama became economically important because of its deposits of nitrates, copper, and other minerals. Disputes over those resources helped lead to the War of the Pacific from 1879 to 1884, after which Chile took control of large desert territories that had previously belonged to Peru and Bolivia.

Today the Atacama remains an important mining region, especially for copper and lithium. It is also one of the world's leading sites for astronomy. Its high elevation, low humidity, minimal cloud cover, and very low light pollution make it especially well suited to astronomical observation. Major observatories in or near the region include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, or ALMA, as well as facilities on Cerro Paranal and La Silla.

The Atacama is also a major destination for tourism and scientific research. Its landscape includes salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Its dry, Mars-like conditions have also made it a useful analogue for testing space exploration technology and studying how life survives in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city can feel, at first, like stepping into a life meant for someone braver than you. The decision usually starts out as an idea: a job offer, school, a relationship, or just a vague urge to start over. On paper, it looks neat and intentional. In practice, it is cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, GPS directions in a flat voice, and the small shock of waking up in a room where the light hits the wall differently. The good parts and the hard parts show up together, so closely tangled that it is hard to pull them apart.

One of the best things about a new city is the chance to see yourself differently. In the place where you have always lived, identity can start to feel fixed by repetition. You are someone's child, someone's friend, the person who orders the usual at the coffee shop or avoids certain streets because of old memories. In a new city, no one knows your history unless you tell it. That anonymity can be lonely, but it can also feel freeing. You can be more social, or more private. You can try new routines, new neighborhoods, even slightly different versions of yourself. The city does not care who you were. It cares how you live in it now.

There is also the simple pleasure of discovery. A new city turns ordinary life into a kind of exploration. Buying groceries becomes a small expedition. You notice the architecture, the slang, the weather, the way people stand in line or talk to strangers. You learn where to get the best bread, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform crowds fastest when it rains. Those details build slowly, and each one makes the place feel less like a map and more like home. Moving reminds you that daily life is not fixed. It can still surprise you.

But the costs are real, and they are often harder to measure than rent or moving trucks. The clearest one is homesickness, though that word can sound too mild for what it is. Homesickness is not just missing people. It is missing the version of yourself that existed so easily around them. In your old city, you knew how to belong without thinking about it. In the new one, belonging takes effort. You have to build a life almost from scratch: find a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, someone to call when something breaks. Even small errands can wear you out when you have to do them without the cushion of familiarity.

There is also the emotional math of distance. Moving often means accepting that love will become less convenient. Friendships that once ran on proximity have to survive on texts, scheduled calls, and expensive visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back and realize that home kept changing while you were away. The city you left does not stay preserved for your return. It moves on, just as you do. There is grief in that.

Maybe that is part of what moving teaches. A life usually grows by being unsettled. A new city gives you freedom, novelty, and growth, and it asks for uncertainty, loneliness, and loss in return. Moving means accepting that trade. If you are lucky, the strange streets become your streets. The costs do not vanish, but over time they can feel less like penalties and more like the price of becoming larger than the life you used to know.

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday that it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients, renewing concerns about cybersecurity in healthcare.

The network, which runs several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region, said it detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. In a statement, officials said the organization contained the incident, opened an internal investigation, and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to determine the scope of the breach.

Preliminary findings indicate that unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records with names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, insurance details, and, in some cases, limited clinical information. Hospital officials said there is no current evidence that financial account or payment card data was compromised, though the investigation is still underway.

“We take the privacy and security of our patients’ information extremely seriously,” the hospital network said in its statement. “Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected.”

The hospital network did not say exactly how many patients were involved, but called the breach “significant.” Affected individuals are expected to be notified by mail in the coming weeks. The organization said it will offer free credit monitoring and identity protection services to eligible patients as a precaution.

Hospital operations have continued during the investigation, though some administrative systems were temporarily taken offline, causing delays in scheduling and access to some online services. Emergency departments and inpatient care were not disrupted, according to officials.

Healthcare organizations remain common targets for hackers because they hold large amounts of sensitive personal and medical data. Unlike stolen credit card numbers, medical records can include permanent identifying details that may be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing attacks.

“This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients,” said one data privacy analyst not affiliated with the hospital network. “Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved.”

Regulators are likely to review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, which requires covered entities to protect patient information and notify individuals when certain breaches occur.

Patients are being advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls referencing their medical care. The hospital network said it is strengthening system security, reviewing access controls, and taking additional steps to prevent a similar incident.

A good teacher knows the subject, but that alone is not enough. Students need more than information. They need someone who can spark curiosity, build confidence, and make learning feel possible. To me, a good teacher brings patience, passion, empathy, and a real ability to make students feel noticed.

Patience matters because students do not all learn in the same way or at the same speed. A good teacher understands that. When a student struggles, they do not give up or get irritated. They explain it again in a different way, use another example, or try a new approach. That kind of patience shows students that struggling is part of learning, not proof that they have failed. For students who already doubt themselves, that can matter a lot. A patient teacher is also teaching persistence.

Passion matters too. Students can usually tell when a teacher genuinely cares about what they teach. That energy spreads. A teacher who talks about literature, science, history, or math with real interest can make even a hard topic feel alive. It gives the classroom energy and makes the lesson stick. It also shows students that learning is not just something to get through. It can be interesting, satisfying, and even joyful.

Empathy is just as important. A good teacher remembers what it feels like to be confused, anxious, or scared of getting something wrong. They know students may be carrying things no one else can see: stress at home, insecurity, loneliness, or pressure to succeed. So they treat students with kindness and respect. They listen. They notice when someone seems unusually quiet or discouraged. Sometimes what helps most is not another explanation but a few words of encouragement at the right time. When students feel understood, they are more likely to join in, take chances, and believe they can improve.

Good teachers also challenge their students. Being kind does not mean expecting less. Some of the strongest teachers ask a lot of their students because they can see what those students are capable of. They push them to think harder, work more carefully, and aim higher than they would on their own. The difference is that they also give support along the way. They do not just ask for excellence. They help students get there.

A good teacher's impact reaches past the classroom. Years later, students may not remember every lesson, date, or formula, but they often remember how a teacher made them feel. They remember the teacher who believed in them when they did not believe in themselves, who sparked an interest they had never thought about before, or who made them feel that their voice mattered. Teaching shapes more than academic growth. It can shape confidence, character, and a sense of possibility.

To me, a good teacher combines knowledge with humanity. They guide, challenge, encourage, and inspire. They help students learn about the world and about themselves. That is why a truly good teacher can stay with someone for life.

# Commit message style guide

Good commit messages make reviews easier, help future maintainers understand why something changed, and make `git log` and `git blame` more useful. Use these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Put a blank line between the subject and the body. The body and footer are optional for trivial changes.

## Subject line

- Limit it to 50 characters. The hard limit is 72.
- Use the imperative mood: "Add retry logic," not "Added retry logic" or "Adds retry logic." A simple test is whether it completes the sentence "If applied, this commit will..."
- Capitalize the first word.
- Leave off the trailing period.
- Be specific. "Fix bug" and "Update code" do not say much. "Fix null check in user lookup" does.

If your team uses prefixes like `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:` from Conventional Commits, use them consistently and keep the full line within the limit.

## Body

Use the body to explain what changed and why, not how. The diff already shows how. Things worth covering include:

- What problem prompted the change
- Why you chose this approach instead of another one
- Any side effects or limitations reviewers should know about

Wrap lines at 72 characters. For lists of separate changes, use bullets with hyphens or asterisks.

## Footer

Use the footer for metadata:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope of a commit

Keep each commit to one logical change. If your subject line needs an "and," consider splitting the commit. Avoid mixing formatting changes with functional changes, because that makes review and reverting harder.

## Examples

**Weak:**
```
fixed stuff
```

**Strong:**
```
Fix race condition in session cleanup

The cleanup job could delete sessions that were being
refreshed concurrently, logging users out unexpectedly.
Acquire a row-level lock before checking expiration.

Fixes #482
```

## Things to avoid

- Vague messages like "WIP," "misc fixes," or "updates"
- Describing the file instead of the change
- References only you understand, like "as discussed"
- Blame or editorializing, like "fix stupid bug"
- Committing generated noise without explaining it

## Final check

Before you commit, ask: would someone reading this in two years understand why the change was made? If not, add more context.

# Tbilisi

Tbilisi (Georgian: თბილისი), historically called Tiflis, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It stands on the banks of the Mtkvari, or Kura, River and had a population of about 1.2 million in the early 2020s, roughly a third of the country's population. It is the main cultural, economic, and transport center of the South Caucasus.

## History

According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded Tbilisi in the 5th century AD after finding warm sulfur springs while hunting. The city's name comes from the Old Georgian word *tbili*, meaning "warm." His successors moved the royal seat there, and Tbilisi grew in importance despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi prospered during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries. It was later sacked several times, including by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire in the early 19th century, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a short period of independence from 1918 to 1921, the city became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991, and Tbilisi has since gone through political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, along with substantial modernization.

## Geography and climate

The city lies in a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at an elevation of about 400 to 770 meters above sea level. Tbilisi has a transitional climate between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

Tbilisi is known for its mix of medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary architecture. The Old Town, or Dzveli Tbilisi, has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Major landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sioni Cathedral, Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda, or "Mother of Georgia," statue overlooks the city from Sololaki Ridge.

The city has many theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian cuisine, including *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is a major part of the city's identity. Tbilisi's nightlife and electronic music scene have also drawn international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is Georgia's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, which opened in 1966, is the city's main rapid transit system, with buses, minibuses, and a cable car adding to the network. Tbilisi International Airport is the country's main gateway.

## See also

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

# Maplewood County school board election draws record turnout

MAPLEWOOD — Maplewood County saw unusually high turnout Tuesday in its school board election, with 41 percent of registered voters casting ballots to choose three board members. It was more than double the turnout in the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters participated, up from about 17 percent two years ago. Several precincts reported lines out the door during the after-work rush, and polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so everyone already in line could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The surge followed a contentious campaign over a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, curriculum, and class sizes. Six candidates ran for three open seats. The race also brought unusually heavy campaign spending for a local contest and a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School ran a registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Others said the issues pushed them to vote.

# Maplewood County school board election draws record turnout

MAPLEWOOD — Maplewood County saw unusually high turnout Tuesday in its school board election, with 41 percent of registered voters casting ballots to choose three board members. It was more than double the turnout in the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters participated, up from about 17 percent two years ago. Several precincts reported lines out the door during the after-work rush, and polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so everyone already in line could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The surge followed a contentious campaign over a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, curriculum, and class sizes. Six candidates ran for three open seats. The race also brought unusually heavy campaign spending for a local contest and a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School ran a registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Others said the issues pushed them to vote.

"Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman in the lead, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who hold the other two winning spots for now. The gap between third and fourth place was fewer than 400 votes, and the elections office said final results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations as it prepares for future high-turnout elections.

"This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1 is a NASA robotic space probe launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program. It was built to study the outer Solar System and, after finishing its original mission, kept going. It is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory built Voyager 1, and a Titan IIIE rocket launched it from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Although Voyager 2 launched first, Voyager 1 took a faster path and reached Jupiter and Saturn earlier. Its route used a rare planetary alignment that let spacecraft visit multiple outer planets through gravitational assists.

Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979. During the flyby, it sent back detailed images of the planet’s atmosphere, including its cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. It also made major discoveries about Jupiter’s moons, especially Io, where it found evidence of active volcanism, the first observed beyond Earth. The mission also returned new information about Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Jupiter’s magnetosphere, and its ring system.

In 1980, Voyager 1 flew past Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a major target because of its dense atmosphere. The spacecraft confirmed that Titan’s atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, though its thick haze blocked detailed views of the surface. Voyager 1 also returned extensive observations of Saturn’s rings, moons, and magnetic environment. Because the Titan flyby required a different path, the spacecraft left the plane of the Solar System and could not continue on to other planets.

After the planetary mission, Voyager 1 began an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region shaped by the solar wind. In August 2012, NASA announced that it had become the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space by crossing the heliopause, where the Sun’s influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Since then, its instruments have continued measuring charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma conditions in this region.

Voyager 1 also carries the Golden Record, a phonograph record of sounds, images, and messages meant to represent life and culture on Earth. It was created as a symbolic message for any future finders and has become one of the mission’s best-known features.

Voyager 1 still communicates with Earth through NASA’s Deep Space Network, although its power supply keeps shrinking as its radioisotope thermoelectric generators lose output. Its mission has been extended several times, and it continues to send back scientific data as it travels farther into interstellar space.

## Pivot Tables User Guide

A pivot table summarizes and analyzes large spreadsheet datasets. You can use it to group data, calculate totals, and spot trends without manually sorting, filtering, or writing formulas.

### When to use a pivot table
Use a pivot table to:
- total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- count records such as customers or orders
- compare values across categories
- rearrange data without changing the original table
- explore patterns in large datasets

### Before you begin
Your source data should:
- be organized in rows and columns
- have a single header row
- contain no completely blank rows or columns
- use consistent data types in each column, such as dates, numbers, or text

Example columns include `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a pivot table
1. Select any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table:
   - New worksheet
   - Existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

A blank pivot table and field list will appear.

### Understanding the pivot table areas
Most pivot table tools have four layout areas:

- **Rows**: categories shown vertically
- **Columns**: categories shown horizontally
- **Values**: calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: limits on the data shown

### Building a basic pivot table
To summarize total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The table will show each region and its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Keep **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing calculations
A value field can usually be summarized in different ways:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change the calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Choose the calculation you want.

### Filtering and sorting
You can refine the results by:
- applying a report filter, such as showing only one year
- sorting row labels alphabetically or by value
- expanding or collapsing grouped items

### Refreshing the pivot table
If the source data changes, refresh the pivot table:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Select **Refresh** from the pivot table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Use clear column names in your source data
- Format numbers for readability, such as currency or percentages
- If dates do not group correctly, check that they are stored as real dates
- Leave the source data unchanged and use the pivot table for analysis

Pivot tables let you reorganize data quickly, which makes reporting and analysis easier.

# Pivot tables: a user guide

## What is a pivot table?

A pivot table summarizes large datasets without formulas. You can group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it to see different views quickly. Use one to answer questions like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before you begin

Make sure your data is ready:

- Include headers. Every column needs a unique, nonblank title.
- Avoid blank rows or columns. They can cause the pivot table to miss data.
- Keep data consistent. Each column should contain one type of information, such as dates or numbers.

## Creating a pivot table

1. Click any cell in your data range.
2. Open the Insert menu and choose Pivot Table.
3. Confirm that the data range is correct.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table: a new sheet or an existing location.
5. Click OK or Create.

An empty pivot table will appear, along with a field panel that lists your column headers.

## Understanding the four areas

The field panel has four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- Rows: categories listed down the left side, such as Product
- Columns: categories listed across the top, such as Quarter
- Values: the numbers being calculated, such as Sum of Revenue
- Filters: fields that limit the whole table to specific items, such as a single year

## Example

Suppose your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag Region to Rows.
2. Drag Month to Columns.
3. Drag Revenue to Values.

The table will show total revenue for each region and month, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the calculation

Numeric fields are usually summed by default. To change that, click the field in the Values box, select Value Field Settings, and choose another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also show values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining your report

- Sort: click the dropdown arrow beside a row or column label.
- Filter: use the same arrow to hide selected items.
- Group: right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- Rearrange: drag fields between areas to change the view.

## Keeping data current

Pivot tables do not update automatically when the source data changes. Right-click the table and select Refresh. If you have added new rows, you may also need to update the source range under Change Data Source.

## Troubleshooting

- Numbers are counted instead of summed: the column probably contains text or blanks. Clean the data and refresh.
- Dates will not group: some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to real dates.

With practice, pivot tables become a fast way to analyze data.

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded, and the ticket counter had long since been stripped of brass. But she pressed her palm against the waiting-room wall as if she were checking a sleeping animal for breath. "I left for the city from this bench," she said. "Your grandfather proposed on that platform." By any architectural standard, the building was unremarkable. To her, it was where her life turned.

I think about that moment whenever someone says old buildings are obstacles: expensive to maintain, awkward to retrofit, standing where something newer could go. They aren't wrong. Old buildings leak. They fight new wiring. They often fail to meet modern codes, and sentiment does not pay for a new roof. I do not think every old structure should be saved. Survival alone does not make a building sacred.

Still, some do deserve saving, for reasons that are practical as much as emotional.

Old buildings hold a kind of memory that no archive can match. A photograph shows you what a street looked like. A building lets you stand inside the proportions people once took for granted. You feel how low the ceilings were, how narrow the stairs, how much the light depended on windows instead of switches. History stops feeling abstract when you have to duck through its doorway.

They also preserve a level of craftsmanship we've mostly stopped paying for. In the library in my hometown, a century-old building where I spent a lot of time as a teenager, someone had carved tiny acorns into the banister. No one had to do that. No budget meeting would approve it now. But generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns, and I think it taught us, without anyone saying it out loud, that ordinary places could be made with care.

Then there's continuity. Neighborhoods made entirely of new construction can feel oddly weightless, like a stage set waiting for a story. Old buildings give a place the feeling of having been lived in. They give newcomers and lifelong residents a shared landmark, even if they remember it differently. That shared point matters. Social fabric is easier to tear than to weave.

And there is the simple matter of waste. The greenest building, as preservationists often say, is usually the one already standing. Demolition throws away the energy and materials already built into a structure, and it fills landfills too.

The train station was eventually torn down and replaced with a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find the spot where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing suggested that a proposal or a departure had ever happened there.

That is what I wish skeptics understood. We do not preserve buildings because stone and timber are inherently precious. We preserve them because they keep the places where our lives took shape. Once they are gone, so are the bench, the palm against the wall, and the proof.

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the forces of William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold Godwinson of England. It was the decisive battle of the Norman Conquest of England and led to the start of Norman rule. Despite its name, the battle was not fought at Hastings itself but about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, near the present town of Battle in East Sussex.

The fighting grew out of a dispute over who should succeed to the English throne. After Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William of Normandy claimed that Edward had earlier promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support that claim. A third claimant, Harald Hardrada of Norway, also invaded England. Harold defeated and killed Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, but his army was left worn out by the campaign.

William crossed the English Channel and landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066. He marched into Sussex, built a prefabricated castle at Hastings, and raided the surrounding countryside, partly to force Harold south. Harold then moved quickly from London with his household troops, the housecarls, and the shire levies known as the fyrd.

The two armies met on Senlac Hill. Harold's men formed a dense shield wall along the ridge. William's army included infantry, archers, and cavalry, in line with Norman military practice. The battle lasted most of the day and was fiercely contested. Early Norman attacks were driven back by the English line. At one point, rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have raised his helmet so his troops could see he was still alive.

A major shift came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while chasing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were real or deliberate, but they let Norman cavalry cut off and destroy sections of Harold's army. Late in the day, Harold was killed. Tradition says he was struck in the eye by an arrow, though the exact cause of his death is uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility killed, resistance gave way.

William's victory cleared the path for his coronation as King William I of England on 25 December 1066. The battle changed English society, the aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. It was later memorialized in sources such as the Bayeux Tapestry, one of the most important visual records of the conquest.

# Transit strike halts buses and trains, leaving thousands of commuters stranded

Union rejects final offer as talks collapse overnight; city braces for a second day of disruption

Hundreds of thousands of commuters looked for other ways to get around Monday after public transit workers walked off the job at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents about 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff, began the strike at 4 a.m. after contract talks with the Regional Transit Authority broke down late Sunday. It is the first systemwide stoppage in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," union president Dolores Reyes said from a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But workers who keep this city moving can't be asked to fall behind on rent while costs rise every year."

The union is seeking a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials offered a 5 percent raise and said they could not meet the other demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

The effects showed up right away. Highways were clogged before sunrise, and traffic officials reported delays as much as 70 percent longer than normal. Ride-share prices jumped, and bike-share stations downtown were empty by 8 a.m. Several major employers told staff to work from home.

At Central Station, usually packed with morning travelers, a small number of people stood reading closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before a friend drove him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and the district said it would keep yellow school buses running because they are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is running at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates say wait times have stretched past two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks at once and offered city staff as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million a day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union said it will keep picketing until it receives a "serious proposal," while the Authority said it is making contingency plans for a prolonged stoppage.

At Central Station, usually packed with morning travelers, a small number of people stood reading closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before a friend drove him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and the district said it would keep yellow school buses running because they are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is running at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates say wait times have stretched past two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks at once and offered city staff as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million a day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union said it will keep picketing until it receives a "serious proposal," while the Authority said it is making contingency plans for a prolonged stoppage.

Some old buildings deserve to be preserved because they still matter. Age by itself is not a reason. A cracked wall or a faded sign is not meaningful just because it survived. But some buildings hold something larger: memory, craftsmanship, identity, and the record of how people once pictured their lives. Preserving them is not about freezing the past. It is about keeping a connection between generations.

I think of old buildings as public memory. Families keep photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can carry feeling in a way facts cannot. Cities and towns need that too. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, church, or row of apartments can show us more about the people who built a place than any plaque can. The width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the wear in the stone steps: these details remind us that history was physical. Someone climbed those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news, for work, for love, or for grief to pass. When those buildings disappear, part of our shared memory goes with them.

Old buildings also deserve preservation because they offer a kind of beauty that is hard to copy. Many were built with patience, durable materials, and a level of care that came from pride, not speed. Even modest structures often show a human touch: uneven bricks laid by hand, wooden floors polished by decades of footsteps, windows placed not only for function but for grace. At a time when so much construction is driven by speed and profit, older buildings remind us that usefulness and beauty can coexist. They teach us to value texture, permanence, and detail.

There is also an ethical reason to preserve them. Demolishing and rebuilding is not always progress. Sometimes it is amnesia dressed up as development. Of course, not every old building can or should be saved. Cities have to change, and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, preserving it is a form of respect. It says the people who came before us are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still mean something. This is especially true of places tied to ordinary people, not just the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a fuller story than a mansion.

What moves me most is the way preserved buildings make time feel layered instead of erased. To walk into an old library or courthouse is to feel, even briefly, that your own life belongs to a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries. It has seen generations come and go and still stands, asking for care, not pity. Preservation, at its best, is an act of humility. It admits that we are not the first people to love a place, and not the last who will need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the docs

Thanks for helping improve the documentation. You can fix a typo, update a screenshot, write a new tutorial, review a pull request, or report a problem you found. Every contribution helps.

## Ways to contribute

- Fix typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples.
- Rewrite confusing sections or add missing context.
- Write tutorials, how-to guides, or reference pages.
- Review pull requests.
- Open an issue if you find a problem and can't fix it yourself.

## Getting set up

1. Fork the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000` to preview your changes live.

For small edits, you can also click **Edit this page** at the bottom of any page and make the change directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, such as `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. The files are written in Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting, then run `npm run build` to make sure the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Please follow these conventions:

- Use plain language. Prefer short sentences and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- Address the reader as "you."
- Use active voice. Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- Put code in code blocks and specify the language for syntax highlighting.
- Use sentence case for headings.
- Make examples runnable. Test every snippet before submitting it.
- Write descriptive link text. Avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

We organize content into four types:

- Tutorials: step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- How-to guides: solutions to specific problems.
- Reference: precise technical descriptions.
- Explanations: background and concepts.

Try to keep each page focused on one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before you submit, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will usually respond within a few days. We may suggest edits. That's a normal part of working together. Once your pull request is approved, your changes are merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Be kind, patient, and respectful. All contributors must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask in the discussion forum or comment on an issue. We're happy to help, especially if this is your first contribution.

The Hanseatic League was a commercial and defensive alliance of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. From the late 12th century to the 17th, it dominated maritime trade in the Baltic and North Seas. At its peak, it linked nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen, and shaped the economy, politics, and urban growth of medieval northern Europe.

The League grew out of the expansion of German merchants, especially from cities like Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and trading privileges abroad. Lübeck, founded in 1143 and well placed between the North and Baltic Seas, became the League's leading city. By the 13th century, merchants from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts, or *Kontore*, in major foreign centers such as London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These outposts worked as warehouses, offices, and legal communities that protected Hanseatic merchants and their interests.

The Hanseatic League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, permanent army, or centralized administration. It functioned instead as a loose association of towns and merchants with shared economic interests. Decisions were made at assemblies called the *Hansetag*, where representatives of member cities negotiated trade policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership remained fluid, and cities took part to different degrees.

Its economic strength came from moving regional goods across long distances. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish came from the east. Cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built efficient shipping networks and used standardized commercial practices that lowered transaction costs and made long-distance trade more reliable. The League also used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, including during its 14th-century conflicts with Denmark.

From the late 15th century onward, the Hanseatic League gradually declined. Stronger territorial states, the shift of trade routes toward the Atlantic, growing Dutch and English competition, and internal divisions all weakened its influence. Its overseas trading privileges were reduced over time, and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities continued to identify with the League, but by the 17th century its political role had largely faded. The last meeting of the *Hansetag* took place in 1669.

The Hanseatic League still shows up in the urban culture, architecture, and commercial law of northern Europe. Former Hanseatic cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn still preserve distinctive brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions tied to the League. In modern historiography, it is often treated as an early example of transnational commercial cooperation and urban networking in European history.

# Bike-share FAQ

## Getting started

How do I rent a bike?
Download the app and create an account. Then find a nearby station, tap "Unlock," and scan the bike's QR code. You can also unlock a bike at a station kiosk with a credit card.

How much does it cost?
- Single ride: $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- Day pass: $12 for unlimited 30-minute rides for 24 hours
- Monthly membership: $20 for unlimited 45-minute rides
- Annual membership: $150 for unlimited 45-minute rides

Discounted memberships are available for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Visit our website to apply.

## Using the service

How long can I keep a bike?
You can ride as long as you want, but any time beyond your plan's included minutes costs $0.15 per minute. For longer trips, dock the bike and check out another one to reset the time.

Where can I return my bike?
Return the bike to any station with an open dock. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest station with space. You'll get a free 10-minute extension.

Do I need to bring a helmet?
Helmets are not provided, but we strongly recommend wearing one. Riders under 16 are required by law to wear a helmet.

Are electric bikes available?
Yes. E-bikes have a green stripe and cost an extra $0.10 per minute. They assist up to 20 mph.

## Safety and problems

What if a bike is damaged?
Check the brakes, tires, and seat before you ride. If something seems wrong, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or use the app. Then return the bike to a dock so it can be taken out of service. You will not be charged for rides under one minute.

What if the bike is lost or stolen?
Lock the bike with the built-in cable lock whenever you stop. Use the "Hold" feature in the app for short stops. If a bike is lost or stolen while checked out to you, report it within 24 hours. If you do not, you may be charged a $250 fee.

Can I ride at night?
Yes. The bikes have built-in front and rear lights that turn on automatically.

## Account help

Can I share my membership?
No. Memberships are personal, and each account can unlock only one bike at a time. Group rides require multiple accounts.

How do I cancel my membership?
Go to Settings > Membership in the app and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end at the close of the billing period. Annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

Who do I contact for help?
Call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available every day from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin system

The editor has a plugin system for extending core features without changing the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a `plugin.json` manifest. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines the plugin metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: unique plugin identifier
- `name`: human-readable name
- `version`: plugin version
- `main`: entry script loaded by the editor

Optional fields include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

When the editor starts, it scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads enabled plugins. The entry script must export an `activate` function. If the plugin exports a `deactivate` function, the editor calls it when the plugin is unloaded or when the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Use `activate` to register commands, subscribe to events, or initialize UI elements. Use `deactivate` to dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins use the `api` object passed to `activate` to interact with the editor. Common namespaces include:

- `api.commands`: register and run commands
- `api.window`: show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels
- `api.workspace`: access open files, project folders, and settings
- `api.editor`: read or modify the active document
- `api.events`: subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement

Example command registration:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and management

Plugins can be installed by copying their directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder or by using the built-in plugin manager. Users can enable, disable, update, or remove plugins from the settings interface.

If a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and continues starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues are reported in the developer console.

### Best practices

- Keep each plugin focused on one job.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs such as `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.
- Avoid blocking work during activation so startup stays fast.

A good plugin should feel like part of the editor, stay lightweight, and fail safely when the context it needs is unavailable.

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I had four hours of countryside ahead of me with nothing to do but look out the window. For the first twenty minutes I was nearly frantic. My hand kept going to my pocket like a tongue to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored, plain and simple.

Then, somewhere after a river I couldn't name, my mind stopped reaching for input and started making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought about in years. I worked out how to restructure a project at work that had been bothering me for weeks. I made up an elaborate backstory for the man asleep across the aisle for no reason at all. By the time we pulled into the station, I felt oddly rested, like I'd actually been somewhere.

I think about that trip a lot because it made me realize what I've been giving up. Boredom used to be hard to avoid. It was in waiting rooms, long car rides, and the dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can erase it almost completely. Every break in the day can be filled with a feed, a podcast, a scroll. I've gotten so good at dodging boredom that I almost forgot it had a use.

I think that use is a kind of internal housekeeping. When nothing is pulling at our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting things out. It makes connections that aren't obvious at first. It brings up worries we've been outrunning and wants we haven't quite admitted to ourselves. Psychologists have linked this kind of mental wandering to creativity and planning, and that fits my experience. My best ideas never seem to arrive while I'm consuming something. They show up in the shower, on walks, while I'm washing dishes, in the unprotected edges of the day.

Boredom also teaches desire in a strange way. If I'm bored long enough, I start to notice what I actually want to do instead of just taking whatever is being offered to me. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody gave me those projects. They came out of the discomfort of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way entertainment never does.

I don't want to overstate any of this. Boredom feels bad, and that's part of what it is. It's a signal, like hunger, that something in us wants engagement. The mistake is answering that signal with whatever is closest. Fast food quiets hunger without nourishing you, and scrolling does the same thing to boredom. It fills the space without giving the mind anything to work on.

So I've been trying a small discipline. I leave my phone in my bag when I'm waiting in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes always feel itchy. Then, almost every time, the restlessness loosens and something opens up. Thoughts I didn't know I was carrying start to come up.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I think it might be more like fallow ground. It looks like nothing is happening. Really, it's where the next thing begins to grow.

Then, somewhere after a river I couldn't name, my mind stopped reaching for input and started making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought about in years. I worked out how to restructure a project at work that had been bothering me for weeks. I made up an elaborate backstory for the man asleep across the aisle for no reason at all. By the time we pulled into the station, I felt oddly rested, like I'd actually been somewhere.

I think about that trip a lot because it made me realize what I've been giving up. Boredom used to be hard to avoid. It was in waiting rooms, long car rides, and the dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can erase it almost completely. Every break in the day can be filled with a feed, a podcast, a scroll. I've gotten so good at dodging boredom that I almost forgot it had a use.

I think that use is a kind of internal housekeeping. When nothing is pulling at our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting things out. It makes connections that aren't obvious at first. It brings up worries we've been outrunning and wants we haven't quite admitted to ourselves. Psychologists have linked this kind of mental wandering to creativity and planning, and that fits my experience. My best ideas never seem to arrive while I'm consuming something. They show up in the shower, on walks, while I'm washing dishes, in the unprotected edges of the day.

Boredom also teaches desire in a strange way. If I'm bored long enough, I start to notice what I actually want to do instead of just taking whatever is being offered to me. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody gave me those projects. They came out of the discomfort of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way entertainment never does.

I don't want to overstate any of this. Boredom feels bad, and that's part of what it is. It's a signal, like hunger, that something in us wants engagement. The mistake is answering that signal with whatever is closest. Fast food quiets hunger without nourishing you, and scrolling does the same thing to boredom. It fills the space without giving the mind anything to work on.

So I've been trying a small discipline. I leave my phone in my bag when I'm waiting in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes always feel itchy. Then, almost every time, the restlessness loosens and something opens up. Thoughts I didn't know I was carrying start to come up.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I think it might be more like fallow ground. It looks like nothing is happening. Really, it's where the next thing begins to grow.

The Weight of a Hamburger

When I was nine, I watched my uncle slaughter a pig. I was supposed to stay in the truck, and of course I didn't. What I remember most is not the blood but the quiet afterward, how ordinary the men seemed once it was over, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. It was delicious, and I could not stop thinking about the pig's eyes.

I've kept coming back to that evening for most of my adult life.

For years I dodged the question the way you dodge a bill you don't think you can pay. I ate chicken breasts sealed in plastic, shaped like nothing that had ever lived. Then I read a book about industrial farming, one of those books written to ruin your appetite, and it did. I became a vegetarian for three years. I meant it, and I was a little insufferable about it.

I believed then, and still do, that suffering matters. Pigs are intelligent, social animals, and they feel fear. If I think a dog's pain matters, I have to explain why a pig's doesn't, and "because it tastes good" is a weak answer. Most meat comes from animals that lived in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them imposed on anything I loved. I've stopped trying to argue my way around that.

But the certainty I had as a vegetarian has worn down, not because the arguments changed, but because life got messier. I spent one winter with relatives whose diet came mostly from what they raised and hunted, and their relationship to meat was nothing like mine. They knew the animals. They thanked them without embarrassment. They wasted nothing. I couldn't honestly say they were doing something worse than I was when I stood in a grocery aisle buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating has a cost. The question is whether you're willing to look at it.

That's where I've landed, uncomfortably. The worst part of modern meat is not the fact of animal death. It's how completely the dying has been hidden from us. Distance makes cruelty easy. If I'm going to eat an animal, I should be willing to know where it lived and how it was killed. If I can't bear to know, that tells me something too.

So now I eat meat rarely and try to know where it comes from. I buy from a farmer whose fields I've walked through. Sometimes I fail. I eat the convenient thing at an airport or a wedding and feel the old pang. I don't think this makes me virtuous. It may only make me a little more conscious of something I still can't fully justify.

I used to want a clean answer, either a rule I could follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking about it. I've come to distrust that wish. Some questions should stay a little open. They should keep bothering you.

I still think about the pig sometimes. I don't think the memory is asking me to stop eating meat. I think it's asking me to stay awake while I do.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a secure seed storage facility on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in 2008 to preserve duplicate seed samples from gene banks around the world and to protect crop diversity from war, natural disasters, equipment failure, climate change, and poor management.

The vault is built into the side of Platåberget, a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen. Its remote Arctic location was chosen for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and the cold climate and surrounding permafrost help protect the seeds even if the power fails. The facility stores seeds at about −18 °C (0 °F), the standard temperature for long-term seed bank conservation.

Sometimes called the world's "doomsday vault," it works as a backup repository rather than a conventional seed bank. It does not own the seeds stored there. They remain the property of the depositing institutions under a "black box" arrangement, so only depositors can access their collections. The system supports national, regional, and international gene banks by giving them an extra layer of security.

The vault was developed by the Government of Norway with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Crop Trust. It can store millions of seed samples covering a wide range of food crops and their wild relatives. Its collections include varieties of wheat, rice, maize, barley, and beans, along with many other agriculturally important species. Preserving that genetic diversity is essential for plant breeding, food security, and adapting crops to changing environmental conditions.

The Seed Vault has already served a practical purpose. In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) became the first institution to withdraw seeds after conflict in Syria disrupted work at its regional gene bank. ICARDA used the seeds to regenerate its collections and later redeposited fresh samples.

Since it opened, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has become an international symbol of efforts to preserve biodiversity and protect the genetic basis of the world's food supply. It is widely regarded as one of the most important facilities for the long-term conservation of crop diversity.

The Weight of Paper

After my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, rubber-banded by year. Mine were in there too: earnest childhood notes about school and a lost tooth that she'd kept for decades. But I kept coming back to her letters, the ones my mother had saved and passed on to me.

Nothing much happens in them. The tomatoes are late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, then Wednesday, then, she wrote, "it seemed to lose interest." I laughed out loud at that, alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice in the slanted blue ink. She had crossed out one word and written another above it, and I could see her pause, then choose. That tiny correction told me more about her than any photograph.

I think that's what we lose when we stop writing letters. Not information, but evidence of attention. A letter shows that someone sat down and kept you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes. They weren't doing it while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. They picked a page, a pen, and you. Now I send dozens of messages a day, and they're quick and warm and useful, but they're also weightless. They arrive in the middle of distraction and get answered the same way. Almost none of them are kept. How could they be?

Letters also demanded a kind of patience, and that patience shaped what people said. You couldn't fire off a feeling and take it back ten seconds later. You had to let a thought run its course, and sometimes it changed as it did. From the shoebox I learned that my grandfather once wrote my grandmother three pages about a quarrel, and the last paragraph contradicts the first. He didn't mean to forgive her when he started. The letter brought him there. A text might have left him angry, or ended the argument in one clipped word.

And there was the waiting. Now we treat waiting as pure cost, a flaw to engineer away. But the days between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox carrying a small, private hope. When something came, it had traveled to reach you. It had a stamp, a smudge, the faint smell of someone else's house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took an hour and a half, much longer than I expected, because I kept finding things I hadn't known I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from disuse. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope into the box, I felt oddly exposed, as if I'd handed over something I could no longer revise.

She wrote back three weeks later. I still have it on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. It says, among other things, that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
This document proposes adding a caching layer to the web API to reduce response times, lower backend load, and improve scalability. The cache will store frequently requested API responses so the system does not have to repeat database or downstream service calls for every request.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Keep data freshness within acceptable limits
- Provide visibility into cache behavior

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data for every endpoint

## Architecture
The caching layer will sit between the API application and backend data sources. For each request, the API will check the cache first. If a valid cached entry is present, the API returns it immediately. If not, the API fetches the data from the source, returns the response, and stores it in the cache.

A distributed in-memory store such as Redis is a good fit because it offers low latency, expiration support, and mature operational tooling. For static or public GET endpoints, a CDN or edge cache can be added later.

## Cache Strategy
The initial implementation will use cache-aside:

1. Client requests a resource
2. API looks up the cache key
3. On a hit, return the cached response
4. On a miss, fetch from the backend
5. Store the result in the cache with a TTL
6. Return the response

This approach is simple and explicit, and it fits read-heavy workloads well.

## Key Design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context, such as locale

Example:

`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item should have a TTL based on how often the endpoint changes:
- Reference data: 1 to 24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1 to 5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30 to 120 seconds

Writes that affect cached resources should also trigger invalidation. For example, when a product is updated, the system should delete or version the related product detail and listing keys. If exact invalidation is hard to maintain, use shorter TTLs instead.

## Reliability Considerations
To prevent cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Negative caching can be used briefly for known missing resources to avoid repeated misses. If the cache becomes unavailable, the API must fall back cleanly to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches should exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Track these metrics:
- Cache hit rate
- Cache miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Reduction in backend requests

Add structured logs and dashboards so the team can monitor how well the cache is working.

## Rollout Plan
Start with a small set of high-read, low-volatility GET endpoints. Measure hit rate and latency improvements, then expand gradually. This phased rollout keeps the initial risk low and confirms the impact with production traffic.

The Library of Alexandria was one of the best-known libraries of the ancient world and a major center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was linked to the Mouseion, or "Temple of the Muses," a research institution established under the Ptolemaic dynasty after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Many details about the library remain uncertain, but it later became a symbol of learning, intellectual ambition, and cultural loss.

It was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to become the main center of Greek culture and scholarship. They collected texts from across the Mediterranean, including works of literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe aggressive acquisition policies. Books brought into the city were reportedly copied, and in some cases the originals were kept for the library while copies were returned to their owners.

The library was part of a broader scholarly community, not just a storage place for scrolls. Scholars working there studied, edited, and compared texts, helping produce critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. The institution attracted leading intellectuals, including Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a large bibliographic catalogue often described as one of the earliest library catalogues in history.

Estimates of the library's size vary widely. Ancient and modern figures range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Scholars also continue to debate how the library was organized and how the main library related to a possible "daughter library" in the Serapeum.

The destruction of the Library of Alexandria is one of the most familiar stories in cultural history, though it probably was not the result of a single catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources connect its decline to several episodes, including Julius Caesar's campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil under Roman rule, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially during the 4th century CE. Most modern historians think the library declined gradually over centuries rather than being destroyed all at once.

The library's legacy lasted far beyond antiquity. It came to represent both the ideal of universal knowledge and the fragility of cultural memory. In modern Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution and its place in world history.

# Hanseatic League

The Hanseatic League, or Hansa, was a commercial and defensive alliance of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It began in the 12th century and reached its peak between the 13th and 15th centuries, when it dominated trade in the Baltic and North Sea regions. Its member cities lay mainly along the coasts of what are now Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and nearby areas.

## Origins

The League grew out of associations of German merchants who traveled together for protection against pirates and bandits. The founding of Lübeck in 1143, and its rise as a gateway to the Baltic, was central to that process. Lübeck's alliance with Hamburg in 1241 is often treated as an early milestone. Over time, many other towns joined, including Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was not a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, permanent treasury, or formal constitution. Instead, it worked as a loose association whose members met in periodic assemblies called the Hansetag, usually in Lübeck. It enforced decisions through collective economic pressure, including trade embargoes, and sometimes through military action. Lübeck is generally seen as the League's leading city and was often called its "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants traded mainly in bulk goods. From the east they brought timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye. From the west and south they imported cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also important. The League maintained major overseas trading posts, or Kontore, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves held special privileges and followed their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power brought it into conflict with rulers who opposed its trading privileges. Its most important war was with Denmark, and it ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370, which confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later, growing competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily weakened its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century onward, the League declined for several reasons. Stronger territorial states emerged, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power expanded, and the League itself was divided. The loss of key privileges further weakened it, including the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598. The last formal assembly met in 1669, although Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left a clear mark on architecture and culture, especially in the brick Gothic buildings found across the Baltic region. Hamburg and Bremen still use "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. Today, the "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days continue to commemorate that heritage.

Hanseatic merchants traded mainly in bulk goods. From the east they brought timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye. From the west and south they imported cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also important. The League maintained major overseas trading posts, or Kontore, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves held special privileges and followed their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power brought it into conflict with rulers who opposed its trading privileges. Its most important war was with Denmark, and it ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370, which confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later, growing competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily weakened its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century onward, the League declined for several reasons. Stronger territorial states emerged, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power expanded, and the League itself was divided. The loss of key privileges further weakened it, including the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598. The last formal assembly met in 1669, although Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left a clear mark on architecture and culture, especially in the brick Gothic buildings found across the Baltic region. Hamburg and Bremen still use "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. Today, the "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days continue to commemorate that heritage.
