The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms and ecological damage in the Great Plains during the 1930s, especially from 1934 to 1936. It grew out of prolonged drought, high winds, and farming practices that left the soil exposed to erosion. The damage was environmental, economic, and social, especially in Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico.

Before the Dust Bowl, much of the Great Plains was covered in deep-rooted native grasses that held the soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large stretches of prairie were plowed for wheat farming and cattle grazing. High crop prices and the belief that "rain follows the plow" pushed many farmers to cultivate marginal land. When drought hit in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil dried out and strong winds carried it away.

Dust storms became the most visible sign of the disaster. Sometimes called "black blizzards," they swept huge clouds of soil across farms, towns, and even distant cities. One of the best known storms came on April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, when a massive wall of dust moved across the southern Plains. The storms ruined crops, buried machinery, killed livestock, and caused widespread breathing problems known as "dust pneumonia."

The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression even harder on farming communities. Farm income collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas, and moved to California and other western states in search of work and better living conditions. These migrants were often called "Okies," though many were not from Oklahoma. Their experiences later appeared in works such as John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath.

The federal government responded with conservation and relief programs under President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. In 1935, it created the Soil Conservation Service to promote farming methods that reduced erosion, including contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and planting shelterbelts of trees. Other programs helped struggling farm families relocate or stay on their land.

Rain returned to the Plains gradually in the late 1930s, easing the worst of the crisis. The Dust Bowl is still remembered as one of the most serious environmental disasters in U.S. history. It is often used as a warning about the effects of unsustainable land use, climate extremes, and the fragility of agricultural systems under ecological stress.

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country, and we wrote letters. They were clumsy, with crossed-out words and drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I still remember the little thrill of seeing her handwriting in the mailbox, and how I read each letter until the folds went soft. We lost touch within a year. Back then, distance could still do that.

My kids will never know that kind of loss, and I’m not sure yet how I feel about it.

I notice what social media has done to friendship most when I try to explain it. I know what my college roommate had for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, that her mother has been sick, that she’s frustrated with her job. I haven’t spoken to her in four years. Is she still my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one, she’s someone I keep up with, which feels like its own category: closeness without contact, intimacy without exchange.

There are real gifts in that. I’ve seen friendships survive moves, career changes, and the ordinary drift that used to end them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I answer while I’m doing dishes. It isn’t the same as sitting across from her, but it still counts. It’s a thread, and threads can be tightened again. When we finally see each other, we don’t have to start from zero.

The costs are quieter, and I’ve felt them more as I’ve gotten older. Social media can make friendship feel performative. I’ve caught myself shaping a moment while I’m still in it, angling the dinner table for a photo, thinking of a caption while a friend is still talking. The experience turns into content, and the friend becomes, at least a little, part of the production.

It has also made affection feel cheap. A like costs nothing. A birthday message prompted by an app takes four seconds. We send these little signals and tell ourselves we’ve done the work of caring, when friendship has always asked for something slower: showing up, sitting through awkward silence, driving across town when someone’s life falls apart. No app has automated that, though it can make it feel optional.

Last winter, a friend I’d only ever liked from afar posted something vague and sad. I almost kept scrolling. Instead, I called her. We talked for two hours, and she cried, and I realized how long it had been since I’d heard her actual voice. The post was a small flare, and I had almost taken it for part of the background.

That’s where I’ve ended up. Social media didn’t ruin friendship, and it didn’t save it either. It widened the net and thinned the rope. What we do with that slack is still up to us. We can treat the feed as the friendship, or use it as a way back into one.

I still have my friend’s old letters, soft at the folds. I don’t want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I do want to write like that again: slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon, I often notice a shift in the office. People are still answering emails, sitting through meetings, and updating spreadsheets, but the energy is different. The sharpness of Monday is gone. Conversations wander. Small tasks take longer than they should. By Friday, it can feel like everyone is acting out work more than really doing it. That feeling has made me more sympathetic to the case for a four-day work week.

What persuades me most is not the appeal of one more day to sleep in, though that does sound nice. It is the recognition that more time at work does not always lead to better work. In many jobs, especially office jobs, productivity is not just a matter of hours logged. Attention runs out. Creativity dulls when people push it too long. Decision-making gets worse when people are tired. We often talk as if endurance were the highest professional virtue, but in practice, clarity matters more. A shorter week accepts something basic about being human: people are not machines, and pretending they are usually produces mediocre work.

I also find the four-day week compelling because it treats rest as something useful instead of something self-indulgent. In many workplaces, exhaustion is worn like a badge of honor. To be overwhelmed is to be important. To be unavailable is to be needed. That logic feels hollow to me. Rest is part of what makes responsibility possible. An extra day away from work can mean time to recover, care for children or parents, make a doctor's appointment without stress, read, exercise, or simply exist outside the demands of employers and inboxes. When people have room to live fuller lives, they often come back to work more focused and less resentful.

There is also, I think, a moral case for the four-day work week. For generations, technological advances have been sold as a path to efficiency and freedom. Yet for many workers, those efficiencies have not turned into more leisure. They have only raised expectations. We can answer messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, but the reward is often just more work. A four-day week points to a different possibility: that the benefits of innovation might finally be shared as time. Time is one of the most precious things a person has.

Of course, not every profession can adopt the same schedule in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service jobs all have practical constraints. A four-day work week is not a fix for every workplace problem. It takes careful planning, staffing adjustments, and a real commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. But those challenges do not weaken the central idea. If anything, they show how badly our assumptions about work need a second look.

To me, the case for a four-day work week is a case for dignity. It asks whether work should consume the best parts of our lives or support them. I do not think people want to contribute less. I think they want to contribute in a way they can sustain, and still have enough of themselves left for the rest of life.

# Wildfire forces thousands to evacuate near Cedar Ridge National Park

CEDAR FALLS, Mont. — A fast-moving wildfire swept through dry timber along the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing more than 3,000 residents to evacuate and leading officials to close the park to visitors.

The fire, called the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and had burned about 14,000 acres by Wednesday morning. Fire officials said it remained 0 percent contained.

"This fire is moving faster than anything we've seen in this area in a decade," Incident Commander Dana Whitfield said at an evening briefing. "Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us."

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. Another 2,000 residents in nearby areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff's deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones across the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with pets, medications, and little else.

"We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could," said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who evacuated with her two children and their dog. "I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back."

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails had been cleared and that rangers had accounted for all registered backcountry visitors. "Visitor safety is our top priority," he said. "We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932."

More than 600 firefighters, backed by helicopters and air tankers, are fighting the flames. Crews have focused on building containment lines near homes and protecting power infrastructure. Officials said two firefighters suffered minor heat-related injuries. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke drifted across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties. They urged children, older adults, and people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said there is a slight chance of rain late Friday, though thunderstorms could also bring dangerous lightning and erratic winds.

Governor Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, freeing up additional state resources. Officials have not determined the cause of the fire, and the investigation is ongoing.

Residents can find updates and shelter information on the county emergency management website.

The first thing I noticed about my new city was how loud the silence felt. In my old apartment, I knew every sound: the radiator knocking, the upstairs neighbor's heavy steps, the bus groaning past at 6:40 every morning. Here, in a sublet that smelled faintly of someone else's cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn't place.

Nobody tells you that moving comes with a kind of small, chosen amnesia. You give up your fluency. I had lived in my old city for nine years and could move through it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had the good tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order when I walked in. In the new city, I got lost on the way to the pharmacy. I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, defeated by brands I didn't recognize. It was humbling, and a little ridiculous, to feel like a child at thirty-four.

That humbling has its own gift. Within a week, my attention sharpened in a way it hadn't in years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rust color that glowed at dusk. I noticed that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere because I didn't have a shorter way yet. A city you don't know makes you pay attention, and I realized how much I had missed the pleasure of simply looking. Routine had worn my days smooth until they started to feel interchangeable.

There were smaller pleasures too. I found a bakery where the owner started saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. I found a river path where, on Sunday mornings, runners and old men with fishing rods shared the same narrow strip of asphalt without bothering each other. Each discovery felt private because no one had pointed me to it. I had found it by wandering.

Still, the costs were real, and they showed up on their own schedule. One came on a Tuesday, when something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, then did the time-zone math and set it back down. Another came in the quiet of the second month, when the novelty wore thin and I understood that friendship doesn't unpack the way boxes do. It builds slowly, through repetition, accident, and simple proximity. I had traded people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that was lonelier than I expected.

I've been here a year now. The bus no longer sounds foreign. I have a place for tomatoes. Last month, a woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I realized I had a week worth describing. I still miss the old city in the way you miss a language you used to speak well.

I've come to think that homesickness is just what it costs to have loved a place, and paying that cost doesn't mean you were wrong to go. Moving taught me that I could be remade, that I was more portable than I had feared. The boxes are long gone. What I carried was never in them.

# Dust Bowl

The Dust Bowl, also called the Dirty Thirties, was a period of severe dust storms in the 1930s that caused major ecological and agricultural damage across the American and Canadian prairies. It grew out of severe drought and decades of farming that left the soil vulnerable to wind erosion, without measures such as crop rotation, cover crops, or terracing.

## Background

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large numbers of settlers moved onto the Great Plains, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by unusually wet weather in the early 1900s. Farmers plowed up the native deep-rooted prairie grasses to plant wheat. High wheat prices during and after World War I pushed that expansion further, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines let farmers cultivate much more land than before. Millions of acres of grassland became cropland, leaving the soil exposed.

## Drought and storms

A series of droughts began in 1930 and returned in waves through 1936 and again in 1939 to 1940. With the grasses that had once held the soil in place gone, high winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous dust clouds. The hardest-hit region included the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma, along with parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On April 14, 1935, remembered as "Black Sunday," a massive storm swept dust across the southern plains and turned day into night. The next day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and even to ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

## Human impact

The storms ruined crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many residents developed "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. Along with the economic hardship of the Great Depression, the disaster forced many families off their farms. About 3.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s, many of them heading to California. Their experiences appeared in works such as John Steinbeck's novel *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs.

## Government response

The federal government created programs to respond to the crisis. The Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935 under Hugh Hammond Bennett, promoted soil-saving methods such as contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, which began in 1934, planted millions of trees in windbreaks, or shelterbelts, across the Plains. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also regulated grazing on public lands.

## Legacy

Rain returned in late 1939, bringing the drought to an end. The Dust Bowl remains one of the worst environmental disasters in American history and helped shape modern soil conservation policy and farming practices.

The Erie Canal is a historic canal in New York State that shaped U.S. economic growth in the 19th century. When it opened in 1825, it created a navigable route between the Hudson River at Albany and Lake Erie at Buffalo, linking the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. That connection cut transportation costs, sped up westward settlement, and helped make New York City the country’s leading port.

The canal was proposed in the early 1800s to solve the problem of moving goods and people across the Appalachian barrier. Overland travel was slow, expensive, and often unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became the project’s main political champion, though critics mocked it as “Clinton’s Ditch.” Construction began in 1817 and relied on thousands of laborers, including many immigrants, who cleared forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks across difficult terrain.

The original Erie Canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. It had 83 locks, which let boats manage an elevation change of more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton marked the event with the “Wedding of the Waters,” a ceremonial trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor in which water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic Ocean.

The canal quickly became one of North America’s most important transportation routes. Freight rates between the Midwest and the East Coast dropped sharply, making it cheaper to move farm products, raw materials, and manufactured goods. Cities and towns along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew fast. The canal also encouraged migration into western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

Its success led to several expansions during the 19th century. In the early 20th century, much of the original route became part of the larger New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918 and combined canalized rivers with new canal cuts. Railroads and highways later reduced its commercial role, but the Erie Canal remained an enduring symbol of American engineering and ambition.

Today, the Erie Canal is used mainly for recreation, tourism, and preservation. It remains an important landmark in the history of transportation, commerce, and U.S. expansion.

Learning a second language as an adult taught me that intelligence is much humbler than I used to think. Before I started, I saw language learning as a test of memory, discipline, and maybe talent. I assumed that if I worked hard enough, I would move steadily from confusion to fluency, picking up grammar rules and vocabulary like tools. Instead, it felt like learning how to be a beginner again.

As a child, I never noticed how much of life depends on language. I moved through my first language without thinking. I could joke, apologize, complain, and tell stories as naturally as breathing. When I started learning another language as an adult, even simple interactions felt heavy. I could have a thought in full color in my head and then realize I only had the words to say it in black and white. In one language I felt articulate and quick; in the other, hesitant and reduced. It was strange to realize how much of what I thought of as myself depended on being able to express myself easily.

That experience made me more patient, with myself and with other people. When you struggle to ask where the bathroom is, accidentally order the wrong food, or misunderstand a question and answer confidently anyway, you start to see communication more generously. I became more aware of how much courage it takes for people to live, work, and raise families in a language that never feels fully their own. Before learning a second language, I admired bilingualism in the abstract. Afterward, I understood it as a daily act of courage.

It also taught me that embarrassment does not destroy you. Adults tend to avoid learning experiences that make them look foolish. Children do not have that option. They are corrected, misunderstood, and exposed all the time, and they keep going. Adults protect competence as if it were fragile. Learning another language forced me to speak badly, mispronounce things, forget words I thought I already knew, and run into the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first it was frustrating. Eventually it was freeing. I realized that improvement depends less on avoiding mistakes than on being willing to live through them.

What surprised me most was how much learning a second language changed the way I listen. In my native language, I often listen for meaning alone. In a second language, I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention. I pay attention to what is said, what is implied, and what I may have missed. That habit followed me back into my first language too. I became slower to assume, quicker to ask, and more aware that understanding another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Learning a second language as an adult did not just give me another way to speak. It changed the way I think about fluency, identity, and patience. It taught me that growth is often awkward, that humility is useful, and that communication is both more fragile and more generous than I once knew. More than anything, it reminded me that becoming a beginner again is not a return to weakness. It is a return to attention.

A record number of voters turned out Tuesday for the Riverton School Board election, a race that usually draws limited attention outside education circles.

The Riverton County Elections Office said more than 18,400 ballots were cast, or about 46 percent of registered voters in the district. Officials said that is the highest turnout ever recorded for a stand-alone school-board election in the community, nearly 5,000 votes above the previous record set in 2017.

Election workers reported steady lines throughout the day at polling sites across the district, with the heaviest traffic in the morning and again after work. Early voting and absentee ballots also rose sharply, adding to the unusually high participation.

“This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see,” said County Elections Director Marisol Vega. “School-board elections typically bring in a smaller slice of the electorate, so this level of turnout is remarkable.”

The high turnout followed months of debate over school funding, classroom overcrowding, campus safety, and the direction of the district’s curriculum. Candidate forums drew large audiences, and community groups on all sides ran extensive outreach campaigns urging residents to vote.

Three seats were open. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his seat, while newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace appeared headed for victory based on unofficial returns released Tuesday night. Final certified results are expected later this week, though the margins were wide enough that observers said the outcome was unlikely to change.

Supporters of the apparent winners said the results showed voters want both stability and new ideas. “People care deeply about what happens in our schools,” Gomez told supporters at a gathering Tuesday evening. “Tonight’s turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families.”

Not everyone agreed on what the results meant, but many residents said the turnout itself was encouraging. Parents, teachers, and retirees interviewed outside polling sites said the school board affects daily life in obvious ways, from academic standards to bus routes and extracurricular programs.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the election showed how much the public cares about the district’s future. “Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate,” Liu said. “That kind of involvement strengthens public education.”

Local analysts said the turnout could shape future elections by showing that school-board races can mobilize voters when the issues feel immediate and personal. For Riverton, Tuesday’s results brought both new leadership and an unusually strong showing at the polls.

VoltNest Energy, a fast-growing home energy startup, has issued a voluntary recall of about 8,200 of its PowerVault S1 home batteries after reports that a defect could cause the units to overheat and create a fire risk.

The wall-mounted batteries are designed to store electricity from rooftop solar panels or provide backup power during outages. They were sold in the United States between March 2024 and September 2026 through solar installers and VoltNest’s website.

In a statement Tuesday, the company said it had received 27 reports of overheating, including five cases of minor property damage such as scorched walls and melted wire insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though VoltNest said two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

The company said the problem appears to come from a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules supplied by a third-party vendor. Under some charging conditions, an internal component can fail and cause excessive heat buildup.

“We are acting out of an abundance of caution,” VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. “Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers, and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible.”

VoltNest told customers to shut down the battery immediately using the system’s main disconnect switch and not to try to repair or remove it themselves. The company said it will offer free inspections, software diagnostics, and replacements where needed. It has also released a firmware update meant to reduce charging stress while replacements are arranged, but said the update does not replace the recall.

The recall was announced with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, which urged owners to follow VoltNest’s shutdown instructions and contact either the company or their installer. The agency said affected units can be identified by serial numbers beginning with PVS1-24 and PVS1-25.

The recall is an early test for VoltNest, a venture-backed company founded in 2021 that has marketed itself as a lower-cost competitor in the growing home battery market. It has expanded quickly as demand for residential backup power has risen alongside more frequent extreme weather and strain on electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could slow the company in the short term, but that its response may matter more than the defect itself.

“Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand,” said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. “But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms.”

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault (Norwegian: *Svalbard globale frøhvelv*) is a secure backup for the world's crop diversity on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago. The media often calls it the "Doomsday Vault." It stores duplicate seed samples from gene banks around the world, so collections are protected if they are lost through accident, mismanagement, war, or natural disaster.

## History

The vault was first proposed in the 1980s and gained support through the work of agricultural scientist Cary Fowler, who later led the Global Crop Diversity Trust, now called the Crop Trust. The Norwegian government paid for construction at a cost of about NOK 50 million. The facility opened on 26 February 2008.

## Location and design

The vault is built into a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole, and sits roughly 130 metres above sea level. That height was meant to keep it above projected sea-level rise. A tunnel about 120 metres long leads to three storage chambers, each built to hold up to 1.5 million seed samples. The total capacity is 4.5 million varieties, or about 2.25 billion seeds.

The surrounding permafrost helps cool the facility, and refrigeration keeps the chambers at about −18 °C, the standard temperature for long-term seed storage. At that temperature, with low moisture, seeds from many major crops can remain viable for centuries or longer. The site was also chosen for its geological stability and low tectonic activity.

## Operation

The Norwegian government owns the vault and manages it with the Crop Trust and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center, or NordGen. Storage is free, with costs covered by Norway and the Crop Trust. Depositing institutions keep ownership of their samples, which are stored in sealed foil packages inside boxes that no one else may open. The vault is only a backup, and only depositors may withdraw their material.

By the early 2020s, the collection held more than 1.2 million samples from nearly every country, including varieties of rice, wheat, maize, barley, sorghum, and many regional crops.

## Notable events

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first major withdrawal. It requested copies of seeds originally held in Aleppo, Syria, after the Syrian civil war disrupted its gene bank operations. The center used them to rebuild collections in Morocco and Lebanon.

In 2017, unusually warm weather and heavy rain sent meltwater into the entrance tunnel. The seeds were not affected, but Norway later funded major upgrades, including waterproofing and better drainage.

## Significance

The vault is a symbol of international cooperation on food security and biodiversity conservation. It also shows that climate change can threaten even facilities built for long-term protection.

I have never trusted habits that arrive with too much ceremony. The ones that help me most are usually small: making coffee before I am fully awake, opening a window even in winter, walking for no particular reason. Walking is the one I rely on most. It asks the least and gives back the most.

I did not always think of walking this way. For a long time, it was just what happened between places: errands, late buses, parking two streets away, crossing campus in bad weather. It was practical, forgettable, sometimes a little irritating. Somewhere along the way, it changed. It stopped feeling like dead time before life and became part of life itself.

Part of the comfort is how plain it is. Walking does not require talent, equipment, or the right mood. It does not ask me to get better at anything. On days when I am tired, restless, or vaguely fried in the modern way, too much screen, too many tabs open in my head, I can still put on shoes and go outside. That simplicity feels corrective. So much of life now is frictionless in ways that make me feel worse: messages arrive instantly, news follows me from room to room, whole afternoons disappear while my body stays still. Walking brings back a useful kind of friction. It reminds me that distance is real, weather is real, my legs are real.

I have noticed that my thoughts change when I walk. At a desk, problems tend to stiffen. They start to feel airless, as if I have handled them too much. Outside, even familiar worries loosen a little. The rhythm of walking gives my mind just enough to do that it stops gripping so hard. I have had ideas come to me in crosswalks, remembered lines I thought were gone, forgiven people a little, forgiven myself a little. None of this feels mystical. Movement just changes the size of a thought. What seems inescapable indoors becomes, outside, one thing among many: a barking dog, a passing train, the smell of cut grass, the sudden authority of a tree.

Walking also brings me back to my senses in the literal sense. I start to notice the world not as backdrop but as company. The same street is never quite the same. There are seasonal changes: wet leaves stuck to the sidewalk, the medicinal brightness of cold air, the worn-out abundance of late-summer gardens. There are small neighborhood dramas too: a child chalking suns on the pavement, someone learning to ride a bicycle, a curtain lifted and dropped. To walk regularly is to become a modest witness. You learn the habits of dogs, the timing of sprinklers, where the first crocuses insist on appearing. Familiarity builds, and with it a quiet affection.

What I value most is that walking offers a kind of progress that cannot be optimized into emptiness. One foot in front of the other is both instruction and outlook. You do not have to leap. You do not have to finish everything today. You move, you pause, you keep going. There is humility in that, and relief.

When I come back from a walk, my life is usually unchanged in any measurable way. The emails are still there, and so are the unanswered questions. But I feel slightly rejoined to myself. I have been reminded that the world extends beyond my preoccupations, and that I can meet it with my own body, at a human pace. For such an ordinary habit, walking has a real power: it brings me back to proportion. More and more, that feels like grace.

## Create calendar event

Creates a new event on a user's calendar.

### Endpoint

`POST /v1/events`

### Description

Creates a calendar event with a title, start time, and end time. You can also include a description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and time zone. On success, the API returns the new event object, including its unique identifier.

### Authentication

Requires a valid bearer token:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

### Request headers

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

### Request body

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

### Body parameters

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title, max 200 characters |
| start | string | Yes | Start date and time in ISO 8601 format |
| end | string | Yes | End date and time in ISO 8601 format |
| description | string | No | Event details, max 5000 characters |
| location | string | No | Event location |
| timezone | string | No | IANA time zone, for example `America/New_York` |
| attendees | array[string] | No | List of attendee email addresses |
| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder definitions |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |
| reminders[].minutesBefore | integer | Yes | Minutes before the event starts |
| recurrence | object | No | Recurrence settings |
| recurrence.frequency | string | No | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or `yearly` |
| recurrence.interval | integer | No | Repeat interval, must be greater than 0 |

### Response

201 Created

```json
{

## Create calendar event

Creates a new event on a user's calendar.

### Endpoint

`POST /v1/events`

### Description

Creates a calendar event with a title, start time, and end time. You can also include a description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and time zone. On success, the API returns the new event object, including its unique identifier.

### Authentication

Requires a valid bearer token:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

### Request headers

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

### Request body

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title, max 200 characters |

| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder definitions |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |

Cyberattack at Riverbend Health exposes records of nearly 380,000 patients

Riverbend, Ohio — Riverbend Health, a regional network of seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, said Tuesday that attackers gained unauthorized access to its systems and may have stolen personal and medical information from about 378,000 current and former patients.

In a statement on its website, the network said it discovered suspicious activity on March 4 after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used for billing records. Riverbend said the intruders appear to have had access since mid-February.

"We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again."

The compromised data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details about diagnoses and treatments, according to the network. Riverbend said it found no evidence that the attackers accessed its electronic health record system, which contains full clinical charts, though the investigation is still underway.

Emergency departments stayed open during the incident, but the network said some scheduling and billing systems were offline for nearly a week. Several patients reported rescheduled appointments and delayed test results.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who receives care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

Riverbend said it has hired an outside cybersecurity firm and notified the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which keeps a public list of large health care breaches. The network said it has not received a ransom demand, though a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is reviewing those claims.

Health care organizations remain frequent targets because medical records contain enough personal information to be useful for identity theft and fraud, security experts say.

"A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes. A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years," said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant who is not involved in the investigation.

Riverbend will begin mailing notification letters next week and is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. Patients can call a dedicated hotline at 1-800-555-0142.

The network advised patients to review insurance statements for unfamiliar services and consider placing fraud alerts on their credit files.

Note: This article is a fictional work created for illustrative purposes.

# Antikythera mechanism

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, often described as the earliest known analog computer. It predicted astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance and tracked cycles in the Greek calendar, including the dates of major Panhellenic games. The device is generally dated to the 2nd or 1st century BCE.

## Discovery

The mechanism was recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. Sponge divers found the wreck in 1900, and salvage operations by the Greek Navy and archaeologists brought up statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. That lump was later found to contain gears and inscriptions. The mechanism is now held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

## Construction

The device was housed in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its bronze components, many thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. Turning a crank drove a system of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, moving pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

The front dial showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac along with a calendar. The Moon's phase appeared on a small rotating, partly silvered ball. The back had two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle, 19 years that align solar years with lunar months, and one for the Saros cycle, about 18 years and used to predict eclipses. Smaller subsidiary dials tracked other cycles, including the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

The Moon's irregular motion, caused by its elliptical orbit, was modeled with a pin-and-slot mechanism that used two gears with offset axes. This matches the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

## Research

Early studies by Valerios Stais, and later by Derek de Solla Price in the 1950s to 70s, established its basic function. X-ray imaging in the 1970s, followed by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project beginning in 2005, used microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging to read much of the inscriptions, which amount to a user's manual. Researchers have also proposed that the device displayed planetary positions, and reconstructions of that gearing have been published, though the evidence is still incomplete.

## Significance

The mechanism is more sophisticated than any other surviving artifact known from the next thousand years, until medieval astronomical clocks in Europe and the Islamic world. Its origin is still debated, with possible links to Rhodes, Corinth, or Syracuse, and to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes. It remains one of the clearest examples of Hellenistic technology and astronomical knowledge.

# Photo Date Renamer

A small command-line tool that renames photo files from the date they were taken, using EXIF metadata. It makes photo libraries easier to sort, search, and archive across folders and devices.

## Features

- Renames photos from the original capture date in EXIF metadata
- Supports common image formats like JPG and JPEG
- Keeps filenames consistent and easy to sort
- Handles duplicate timestamps by adding a counter
- Can process one folder or recurse through subfolders
- Includes a dry-run mode so you can preview changes first

## Why use it?

Cameras and phones often create filenames like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`. Those names stop being useful once the files are mixed into a larger library. This tool replaces them with timestamp-based names such as:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

The result is readable, sorts cleanly, and helps avoid confusion when you combine photos from multiple devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package is published, you may also be able to install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

Rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

Process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

Preview changes without modifying files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

Use a custom filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed with this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos have the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix so files are not overwritten.

## Missing metadata

If a file does not have a valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it by default and reports it in the summary output. Depending on configuration, future versions may optionally fall back to the file's creation or modification time.

## Safety

- Does not overwrite an existing file without warning
- Supports dry runs for safe previews
- Reports renamed, skipped, and failed files at the end

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you find a bug or want to suggest a feature, open an issue with sample filenames, expected behavior, and your platform details.

## License

MIT License.

A regional airline canceled dozens of flights this week, saying it does not have enough qualified pilots to keep its schedule running. The disruption left passengers looking for other ways to travel.

The airline, which flies short routes between smaller cities and major hubs, said it cut the flights to stay within federal safety, staffing, and crew-rest rules. Officials said staffing had dropped below the level needed to operate the full schedule reliably.

"We regret the inconvenience to our customers, but safety remains our top priority," the airline said in a statement released Tuesday. "Like many regional carriers across the industry, we are facing significant challenges in recruiting and retaining pilots."

The cancellations hit routes in several states. Some passengers found out only hours before departure that their flights had been removed from the schedule. At several regional airports, travelers reported long lines at customer service desks while airline staff tried to rebook them on later flights or arrange ground transportation.

"I was supposed to fly out this morning for a business meeting, and now the next available flight isn't until tomorrow," one passenger at a regional airport said. "It's frustrating because there weren't many backup options."

Analysts say pilot shortages have become a serious problem for regional airlines. These carriers often serve as a stepping stone for pilots before they move to larger airlines with better pay. Regional airlines have had trouble competing on wages and quality of life, especially as air travel demand has recovered and bigger carriers have stepped up hiring.

The problem has grown worse because of mandatory retirement rules, higher training costs, and stricter experience requirements for new pilots. Those factors have reduced the number of available crew members, especially for smaller carriers serving less profitable markets.

Aviation consultant Mark Ellison said regional airlines are often hit harder because they have fewer backup staff. "When a major airline loses a few pilots, it can sometimes absorb that disruption," he said. "For a regional carrier, even a small staffing gap can force widespread cancellations."

The airline said it is offering travel waivers and refunds to affected customers and is working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible. Company officials said hiring is underway, including recruitment bonuses and expanded training partnerships.

For communities that rely on regional air service, the cancellations raise concerns about how stable those connections are. Local business leaders and airport officials say long service cuts could hurt tourism, business travel, and local economic activity.

Passengers are being advised to check their flight status before leaving for the airport, since more schedule changes are possible in the coming days.

Redwood County, Calif. — A fast-moving wildfire near Redwood Canyon National Park forced mandatory evacuations Tuesday as firefighters contended with dry conditions, gusty winds, and rugged terrain that officials said were driving the blaze.

The Canyon Ridge Fire started late Monday afternoon about five miles east of the park’s southern boundary and had grown to an estimated 7,800 acres by Tuesday evening, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Containment remained low as crews worked to protect homes, campgrounds, and critical infrastructure in nearby mountain communities.

Authorities ordered evacuations for residents of Pine Creek, Alder Grove, and Millstone, along with several rural neighborhoods along Highway 86. Parts of the park’s gateway communities were also placed under an evacuation warning, and visitors were told to be ready to leave on short notice.

"This fire is moving rapidly and conditions can change minute by minute," Incident Commander Laura Mendes said during an evening briefing. "Our top priority is life safety, getting people out of harm’s way and giving firefighters the room they need to work."

No deaths or serious injuries had been reported as of Tuesday night, though officials said several structures were threatened and at least two outbuildings had been destroyed. The cause of the fire remained under investigation.

A section of Highway 86 was closed to non-emergency traffic, and park officials temporarily closed the national park’s southern entrance, along with several backcountry trails and campgrounds. Rangers began escorting campers from affected areas early Tuesday, while smoke filled nearby valleys and reduced visibility across the region.

The National Weather Service issued a red flag warning for the area, citing low humidity, high temperatures, and wind gusts that could exceed 30 mph. Fire officials said those conditions were expected to continue into Wednesday, making containment harder.

More than 600 firefighters, supported by air tankers, helicopters, and bulldozers, were assigned to the incident. Crews worked overnight to cut containment lines and protect structures in evacuation zones.

At an evacuation center set up at Redwood County High School, displaced residents arrived with pets, medications, and a few personal belongings. Volunteers handed out food, water, and blankets as families waited for updates.

"We grabbed what we could and left," said Pine Creek resident Maria Lopez, who evacuated with her husband and two children. "You could see the glow on the ridge, and the wind was just pushing it closer."

Officials urged residents to monitor emergency alerts and stay away from the area. "If you have been told to leave, leave now," Mendes said. "Do not wait to see the fire."

# Commit message style guide

A commit message should say what changed and why. That gives future readers enough context to follow the project history without reading every diff. Keep messages clear, consistent, and concise.

## Structure

Use this format:

```text
<type>: <short summary>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

### 1. Short summary

- Keep it to 50 characters or fewer when possible.
- Use the imperative mood: “add”, “fix”, “remove”, not “added” or “fixes”.
- Start with a lowercase type followed by a colon.
- Do not end the summary with a period.

Examples:

- `fix: handle null response in user service`

## Installation

`csvparser` requires Python 3.8 or later and is available as a standard Python package.

Install it with `pip`:

```bash
pip install csvparser
```

If you're working inside a project, use a virtual environment first:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install csvparser
```

To verify the installation:

```bash
python -c "import csvparser; print(csvparser.__version__)"
```

To install from source, clone the repository and install in editable mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/csvparser.git
cd csvparser
pip install -e .
```

Editable mode is useful during development because local code changes are available immediately without reinstalling the package.

## Quick start

`csvparser` reads CSV files and returns rows as dictionaries.

Suppose you have a file named `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,30,London
Bob,25,Paris
Charlie,35,Berlin
```

You can parse it like this:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")
rows = parser.read()

for row in rows:
    print(row)
```

Output:

```python
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': '30', 'city': 'London'}
{'name': 'Bob', 'age': '25', 'city': 'Paris'}
{'name': 'Charlie', 'age': '35', 'city': 'Berlin'}
```

### Reading rows one at a time

For large files, iterate over the parser instead of loading the whole file into memory:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")

for row in parser:
    print(row["name"], row["city"])
```

### Custom delimiter

If your file uses a delimiter other than a comma, pass it when you create the parser:

```python
parser = CSVParser("data.tsv", delimiter="\t")
rows = parser.read()
```

### Header validation

You can require specific column names:

```python
parser = CSVParser(
    "people.csv",
    required_columns=["name", "age", "city"]
)

rows = parser.read()
```

If any required columns are missing, the parser raises an error before processing starts.

## Error handling

Wrap parsing in a `try`/`except` block to handle invalid files:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser, CSVParserError

try:
    rows = CSVParser("people.csv").read()
except CSVParserError as exc:
    print(f"Failed to parse CSV: {exc}")
```

## Next steps

Once basic parsing works, you can add value checks, convert string fields to integers, floats, or dates, skip empty lines, or plug parsing into ETL scripts or web backends.

For full API details, see the project documentation or the docstrings in the source code.

The Fifth Day

For six years, Sunday evenings came with a low hum of dread. Nothing was exactly wrong. The job was fine, and my colleagues were kind. But the weekend kept disappearing. Saturday went to errands and recovery. Sunday went to thinking about Monday. I was living around my life instead of in it.

Then my company ran a pilot: four days a week, same pay, same output expectations. I assumed there had to be a catch. Either the days would quietly stretch to ten hours, or I'd come back to a pile of Friday's unfinished work.

What happened was stranger than that. The work contracted to fit the week. Meetings that used to drift for an hour got to the point in twenty minutes. We stopped setting up meetings to talk about other meetings. With only four days, people protected their time. They said no more often, and everything that mattered still got done.

The research since then matches what I felt. In the 2022 UK pilot, involving about 61 companies and roughly 2,900 workers, most firms kept the shorter week afterward. Employees reported less burnout and better sleep, and revenue stayed steady. Earlier trials in Iceland found much the same thing. That doesn't mean every workplace can do this. It does weaken the assumption that more hours automatically create more value.

The deeper problem is the assumption itself. The five-day week comes from an industrial model, when output tracked hours on the factory floor. Most of us do not work that way anymore. Knowledge work depends on attention, and attention does not increase in a straight line with time. For me, the fifth day was often the one where I was technically present but mentally gone, replying to emails so someone could see I was there.

What I got back was not only rest, though rest mattered. I got back ordinary life. I could go to the dentist without performing surgery on my calendar. I could cook an actual Friday dinner. I spent a long afternoon with my father, who is older now than I am ready for, and I realized how much of our relationship had been squeezed into scraps of leftover time. A day off is less a luxury than room for the parts of life that make you more than an employee.

The fairness concerns are real. A four-day week is harder to arrange for nurses, teachers, and restaurant staff, whose work cannot be compressed by cutting meetings. That means it has to be designed carefully, with staggered shifts, more hiring, and honest measurement. It is not a reason to avoid trying it where it can work. And in some places, people will simply squeeze five days into four longer ones, which misses the point. The goal is not the same hours packed into fewer days. The goal is fewer hours, used well.

I do not think a four-day week fixes everything. Bad managers will still be bad, and pressure will still find new places to settle. But I came out of that pilot with a clearer sense of what work is for. It is part of a life. It should not be the thing the rest of life has to orbit.

These days, Sunday evenings are quiet. That matters to me more than any productivity statistic.

The Teacher Who Waited

In seventh grade, I had a math teacher named Mr. Okafor who did something that drove me crazy at the time: he would not give me the answer.

I was stuck on a word problem about two trains, so I raised my hand with the confidence of someone who assumed adults were there to clear things up fast. He came over, looked at my paper, and asked, "What do you know so far?" I told him nothing. He said, "Great. Let's write that down."

Then he waited.

Not in an impatient way, and not with a sigh. He just stood there, calm as if he had all afternoon. Eventually, just to fill the silence, I started saying what I did know: the trains left at different times, one was faster. Somewhere in the middle of hearing myself say it, I saw the answer.

I've thought about that silence for years. It taught me that a good teacher's job is not just to hand over knowledge. It's to help build the person who can find it.

Of course the material matters. A teacher who doesn't understand the subject can't guide anyone through it. But I've known brilliant people who were bad teachers because they had forgotten what it feels like not to know. Expertise can make people impatient with confusion. Mr. Okafor treated confusion like a normal place to be, maybe even a useful one. He never made me feel stupid for standing there.

A good teacher also makes it safe to be wrong. In his classroom, mistakes went on the board for everyone to look at, and we examined them with curiosity instead of judgment. "Interesting," he'd say. "Where did this go sideways?" We learned to track down our own errors like detectives instead of hiding them like evidence. I've carried that into adulthood, where admitting a mistake early can be the difference between a small problem and a disastrous one.

There's another quality that's harder to pin down. Good teachers believe in you a little before you've earned it. Mr. Okafor once handed me a problem from a competition packet meant for older students and said, "I think you'd enjoy this one." I didn't solve it. But I spent a week trying, and I still remember what it felt like to be taken seriously. His expectation felt like a loan, and I worked hard to repay it.

I've had teachers since then who were more charismatic, more entertaining, more widely admired. Some of them were wonderful. But when I think about the people who changed the way I think, I come back to the man who stood beside my desk and let the silence stretch until I filled it myself.

Teaching this way takes restraint. It would have been faster for him to show me the solution, and I probably would have felt grateful for ten minutes. Instead he gave me something slower that lasted longer: the experience of figuring it out, and the quiet realization that I could.

I don't remember the answer to the train problem. I remember the waiting. Maybe that is the point.

Regional carrier Skyline Air said Monday that it will cancel about 120 flights over the next six weeks because it does not have enough qualified pilots.

The cuts will hit service to eight mid-sized and rural markets, including Cedar Falls, Marlow County, and Pine Harbor. Three of those communities will lose daily service altogether until at least mid-March, the company said.

"We deeply regret the disruption to our customers and the communities we serve," said Dana Whitfield, Skyline Air's chief operating officer. "We have exhausted every option to cover these routes safely and within federal duty-time regulations. Without enough pilots, we cannot operate the schedule we promised."

Skyline said it has lost nearly 15 percent of its pilots over the past year as many left for major airlines offering higher pay, signing bonuses, and quicker paths to international routes. The airline now employs about 340 pilots, down from 400 last January.

Analysts said Skyline's situation reflects a broader national shortage. A wave of retirements among veteran pilots, along with a federal rule requiring airline captains to log 1,500 flight hours, has tightened the pipeline of new hires. Regional airlines, which often train pilots who later move to larger carriers, have been hit especially hard.

"Regionals are the farm system of the industry," said Marcus Tran, an aviation consultant. "When the big airlines hire aggressively, the regionals bleed talent. Then the small towns that depend on them lose air service, and it's very hard to get it back."

For passengers, the effect was immediate. At Cedar Falls Regional Airport on Monday, traveler Priya Natarajan said her flight to a family wedding was canceled with two days' notice.

"I got a text and an email, and that was it," she said. "Now I'm looking at a five-hour drive to the nearest hub."

Local officials said they were worried about longer-term effects. Cedar Falls Mayor Tom Hendricks said reliable air service is important for attracting employers and supporting local businesses.

"Losing flights isn't just an inconvenience," he said. "It affects our economy."

Skyline said affected passengers will get full refunds or be rebooked on partner airlines when possible. The company also announced a retention package that includes raises of up to 18 percent and a tuition-assistance program for aspiring pilots.

Whitfield said the airline hopes to restore full service by April but would not guarantee a timeline.

## Public bike-share service FAQ

### 1. What is the bike-share service?
The bike-share service is a simple, low-cost way to get around the city. You can unlock a bike at one station, ride where you need to go, and return it to any station in the network with an open dock.

### 2. How do I sign up?
Sign up in the app or on the website. Create an account, choose a pass or membership, and add a payment method. After that, you can unlock bikes from the app.

### 3. What types of passes are available?
We offer single rides, day passes, and monthly or annual memberships. Short-term passes work well for visitors, while memberships make more sense for regular riders. Current prices are listed in the app and on the website.

### 4. How do I unlock a bike?
Open the app, find a nearby station or available bike, and scan the QR code or enter the bike number. The lock will release automatically. If it doesn't, contact customer support.

### 5. Where can I return a bike?
Return bikes to any official bike-share station with an open dock. Make sure the bike locks into place, then wait for confirmation in the app so you don't get charged extra.

### 6. Is there a time limit for rides?
Yes. Ride limits depend on the pass or membership you choose. If you go over the included ride time, extra fees may apply. You can check your ride details in the app at any time.

### 7. What if a station is full?
If your destination station is full, the app will show nearby stations with open docks. Some riders may also get a grace period to return the bike at the next closest station.

### 8. What should I do if a bike is damaged?
If you notice a problem before or during your ride, report it in the app right away. If needed, choose another bike. This helps keep the fleet safe and in good condition.

### 9. Do I need to wear a helmet?
Helmets are strongly recommended for all riders. Local law may also require them for certain age groups, so check the rules in your area before you ride.

### 10. What happens if a bike is lost or stolen?
If your bike is lost or stolen during your rental, contact customer support right away. File a police report if required. Charges may apply until the bike is recovered or the case is resolved.

### 11. How can I contact customer support?
You can reach customer support through the app, the website, or by phone. Check the Help section for current contact details and service hours.

I grew up in a family where meat was as ordinary as furniture. It was always there and almost never questioned. We had roast chicken on Sundays, bacon on weekends, burgers in the summer. No one talked about whether eating animals was right or wrong because it did not seem like a real question. Meat was food, and food was what kept a family going and brought us to the table. If anyone got thanks, it was the person who cooked, not the animal that had died.

That changed for me slowly, through a buildup of small discomforts. I remember looking at packaged meat in the grocery store and, maybe for the first time, noticing the strange gap between the product and the life it came from. The plastic wrap felt meant not just to preserve the meat, but to keep me from thinking too hard about it. Once I started thinking, it was hard to stop. I realized my appetite depended on looking away. I liked animals in the abstract, and when they were on my plate, I preferred not to picture them at all.

That, to me, is where the ethical problem starts. Most of us would say animal suffering matters, at least to some degree. We can recognize pain in a dog, fear in a cow, agitation in a chicken. Yet the food system often treats these animals as production units instead of living creatures with experiences of their own. If causing unnecessary suffering is wrong, industrial meat production is hard to defend. The confinement, mutilation, and slaughter happen on such a huge scale that it is hard to even take in, and that may be part of why it continues. Cruelty is easier to take part in when branding, routine, and convenience hide it from view.

At the same time, I do not want to flatten this into a simple moral test. Eating meat is tied up with culture, class, geography, and memory. For some people it is tradition. For others it is survival, health, or the lack of realistic alternatives. I do not think it makes sense to act as if everyone is choosing from the same set of options. Someone buying cheap meat to feed a family under financial pressure is in a different position from someone treating animal products as a luxury. Moral judgment without social context can turn into self-congratulation.

Still, complexity is not an excuse for indifference. The fact that no one can live perfectly does not mean no one has to try. I do not have a pure or final answer. I eat less meat than I used to, and when I do eat it, I feel the weight of that choice more clearly. For me, the ethics of eating meat is not only a question of whether killing animals can ever be justified. It is also a question of whether I am willing to let comfort shut down attention. If ethical eating is possible at all, I think it starts there: looking steadily at what feeds us, what it costs, and who bears the cost.

At thirty-four, I stood in a bakery in Lisbon rehearsing a sentence. I wanted a coffee and a custard tart. I'd practiced on the walk over, but when the woman behind the counter looked up, the words vanished. I pointed and said "this" twice. She smiled kindly, the way you smile at a child, and I felt my face go hot.

That was the first thing Portuguese taught me: how much of my adult identity depended on sounding competent. At home, people came to me for answers. In that bakery, I had the vocabulary of a toddler and the pride of a department head, which was a miserable combination.

For months, I felt like a reduced version of myself. I couldn't joke or argue or make the offhand comment that makes someone distinct. I'd thought my personality was a stable thing. It turned out to rely a lot on grammar. What came through instead was something plainer: patient, a little earnest, often confused. Strangely, people liked that person. My neighbor Dona Fernanda, who was seventy and had never left Portugal, corrected me with great ceremony. "Not eu sou cansado," she'd say. "Estou cansado. You are tired, but you are not made of tired." I've never forgotten the difference between permanent and temporary states, and I think about it in English too.

The second thing it taught me was how to listen. In my first language, I listened lazily, half composing my reply. In Portuguese, I had to catch every word as it came. I started noticing tone, gesture, and the pauses people left for each other. I became a better listener in both languages, and I was a little embarrassed by how much I'd missed before.

It also taught me that mistakes don't kill you. Once, at dinner, I told the table I was "very constipated" when I meant embarrassed. The words are false friends, and I will leave it there. Everyone laughed, someone refilled my glass, and I felt more included than I had all week. I learned that failing in public usually makes people warmer toward you. I'd spent years avoiding the thing that might have loosened me up.

Progress stayed invisible until, suddenly, it wasn't. For a long time I felt stuck. Then one afternoon I realized I'd followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed at the right moment. No one announced it. No one handed me a certificate. A door I hadn't known was closed was just open.

I still make errors every day, and I still hear the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. I don't hear it as pity anymore. I hear hospitality, extended to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

What I carry from those years isn't fluency, exactly. It's a willingness to be the smaller person, to point and say "this" and try again. That person was never lesser. He was learning, which was the one thing I'd stopped letting myself do.

# Erie Canal

The Erie Canal is a historic canal in New York State that connects the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Completed in 1825, it was the first navigable waterway to link the Atlantic coast with the Great Lakes. It played a major role in the economic growth of the United States in the nineteenth century.

## History

Plans for a canal across upstate New York had circulated since the late eighteenth century, but the project moved forward under Governor DeWitt Clinton. After federal support fell through, he secured state funding in 1817. Critics mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began on July 4, 1817, in Rome, New York.

The canal was built mostly by hand by laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, using horses, oxen, and simple tools. Engineers such as Benjamin Wright and James Geddes had little formal training and learned as they worked, developing methods to clear forests, stumps, and swampland. The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. Its 83 locks handled an elevation change of about 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial voyage and poured Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in what became known as the "Wedding of the Waters."

## Economic and social impact

The canal sharply cut the cost and time required to move freight. The cost of shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City dropped from about $100 to about $10, and travel time fell from weeks to days. Midwestern farm products moved east, while manufactured goods and settlers moved west.

New York City overtook ports such as Philadelphia and Boston and became the country's leading commercial center. Cities along the canal, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew quickly. The route also became a center of social change. It was closely tied to religious revivalism, the women's rights movement, and abolitionism, which led some historians to call western New York the "burned-over district."

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged between 1836 and 1862. From 1905 to 1918, it was replaced by the larger New York State Barge Canal, which used rivers and lakes as part of its route. In the twentieth century, railroads, highways, and the St. Lawrence Seaway reduced commercial traffic on the canal.

Today, the canal is used mainly for recreation, including boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress designated the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to help preserve its history. The canal is still operated by the New York State Canal Corporation.

## See also

- DeWitt Clinton
- Great Lakes
- Hudson River
- Transportation in New York

I used to think cars meant freedom. When I was younger, a city seemed to start where the traffic got thick: bright lights, constant motion, engines idling at red lights. A busy street felt important. If everyone was trying to get there, that had to be where life was.

The older I get, the more I notice what traffic takes from a place. Conversations get cut off by sirens. Fumes hang in the air on summer afternoons. People squeeze down narrow sidewalks while rows of cars sit motionless in the street. So when I think about whether city centers should ban cars, I lean yes, not because I hate cars, but because I think those spaces should belong to people first.

What changed my mind was not a statistic, though there are plenty on pollution and safety. It was a feeling. In the places I have visited where cars were limited or missing, I felt the difference almost at once. People walked in the street without fear. Children moved the way children do, unpredictably, and no one seemed irritated by their presence. Outdoor tables felt like places to stay a while, not little islands in the noise. The city did not feel empty without cars. It felt more fully inhabited.

A city center is more than a route through town. It is where a city shows itself to itself. It is where tourists get their first impression, where office workers buy lunch, where older people cross the road, where protests gather, where strangers briefly become a crowd. If that space is dominated by vehicles, that says something bleak about our priorities. We are choosing speed over encounter, convenience over community.

Banning cars from city centers is not simple. Disabled people, delivery drivers, emergency services, and people commuting from places with poor public transit cannot be ignored. Small businesses may worry about losing customers. Any policy that brushes past those realities will feel less like progress than punishment.

So I do not mean an absolute or careless ban. I mean a careful one, with exemptions, dependable public transit, better cycling infrastructure, and a clear plan for deliveries and access. The point is not to punish drivers. It is to decide what kind of city life we want to make easier.

Cars are useful. But city centers are too valuable to shape around them. If we remove cars from those spaces carefully, fairly, and with real alternatives in place, we may find that it is not much of a sacrifice after all. We may simply be getting something back: cleaner air, quieter streets, and the sense that the center of a city belongs to the people in it.
