I still remember walking into my local public library as a child and feeling that I had stepped into a place unlike any other. It was quiet, but not formal. It felt full of possibility as much as books. I couldn't have explained then what the library meant to me, but I knew I was welcome there without having to buy anything, prove anything, or be anything in particular. I've carried that feeling with me ever since, and it's part of why I still care so much about public libraries.

Now that almost any fact or article can be pulled up on a phone in seconds, it's easy to think of libraries as useful once, but no longer necessary. If books can be ordered online and information found instantly, what is a library for? To me, the answer is straightforward: a public library does more than hold information. It gives people access to knowledge, a place to be, and a visible sense of community.

What matters most to me is that a public library is one of the few spaces left that is genuinely open to everyone. So much of modern life comes with the expectation that you pay to remain there. Cafes, stores, and entertainment spaces all carry some version of that rule. A library asks only that you respect the space and the people in it. You can sit, read, think, learn, or just rest. That kind of openness is rare, and it says something generous about what a community thinks people deserve.

Libraries matter for another reason too: access to information is nowhere near as equal as we like to imagine. Not everyone has reliable internet, a quiet place at home, up-to-date technology, or money for books and subscriptions. For many people, the library fills those gaps. It offers computers, internet access, job search help, research support, language learning, and educational programs. For a student, it can be a place to study. For someone looking for work, it can be where a resume gets written and submitted. For an immigrant, it can be a way into a new community. For someone who is lonely, it can simply be a place where they don't feel quite so alone.

I also value libraries because they make room for a slower, more thoughtful kind of discovery. Online, algorithms usually steer us toward what they think we'll already like. In a library, you can wander. You can pull a book off the shelf because the title catches you off guard, or because it's sitting beside the one you came for. Those small accidents can change what a person reads, thinks about, or cares about. Libraries are a reminder that learning isn't only about speed. It's also about curiosity.

More than anything, public libraries still matter because they represent a democratic idea: knowledge should not belong only to the people who can afford it. A library pushes back, quietly, against exclusion. It treats stories, facts, history, imagination, and opportunity as things that should be shared.

That's why libraries still feel essential to me. They are not leftovers from an earlier time. They are living promises. In their own modest way, they show what a community can be when it chooses to make room for everyone to enter, stay, and grow.

# Create event

Create a new event on a calendar.

## Endpoint

```http
POST /v1/calendars/{calendar_id}/events
```

Authentication: Bearer token with the `calendar.events.write` scope.

## Path parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `calendar_id` | string | Calendar ID. Use `primary` for the user's default calendar. |

## Request body

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | string | Yes | Event title, up to 200 characters. |
| `start` | string | Yes | Start time in ISO 8601 format, for example `2025-07-01T14:00:00Z`. |
| `end` | string | Yes | End time. Must be after `start`. |
| `timezone` | string | No | IANA time zone, for example `America/New_York`. Defaults to the calendar's time zone. |
| `description` | string | No | Event details, up to 5,000 characters. |
| `location` | string | No | Physical address or meeting URL. |
| `attendees` | array | No | List of objects with an `email` field and an optional `optional` boolean. |
| `reminders` | array | No | List of objects with `method` (`email` or `popup`) and `minutes_before`. |
| `recurrence` | string | No | RRULE string, for example `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=10`. |
| `send_notifications` | boolean | No | Whether to email invitations. Default is `true`. |

## Example request

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/calendars/primary/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Project Kickoff",
    "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
    "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
    "location": "https://meet.example.com/kickoff",
    "attendees": [
      { "email": "jordan@example.com" },
      { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true }
    ],
    "reminders": [{ "method": "popup", "minutes_before": 10 }]
  }'
```

## Success response

Status: `201 Created`

```json
{
  "id": "evt_8f3k29x",
  "calendar_id": "primary",
  "title": "Project Kickoff",
  "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
  "status": "confirmed",
  "attendees": [
    { "email": "jordan@example.com", "response": "pending" },
    { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true, "response": "pending" }
  ],
  "created_at": "2025-06-20T09:12:44Z",
  "url": "https://calendar.example.com/events/evt_8f3k29x"
}
```

## Errors

| Status | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Missing required field, malformed date, or `end` is before `start`. |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | Token is missing, invalid, or expired. |
| 403 | `insufficient_scope` | Token does not have write permission for this calendar. |
| 404 | `calendar_not_found` | The specified calendar does not exist. |
| 409 | `conflict` | An identical event already exists when you use an idempotency key. |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | Too many requests. Retry after the time in the `Retry-After` header. |

## Notes

- Include an `Idempotency-Key` header if you need to retry a request without creating duplicates.
- Rate limit: 60 requests per minute per user.
- You can add up to 200 attendees to an event.
- For all-day events, pass dates only, for example `2025-07-01`, for `start` and `end`. The `end` date is exclusive.

}

|---|---|---|

| 401 | `unauthorized` | Token is missing, invalid, or expired. |
| 403 | `insufficient_scope` | Token does not have write permission for this calendar. |
| 404 | `calendar_not_found` | The specified calendar does not exist. |
| 409 | `conflict` | An identical event already exists when you use an idempotency key. |

Friendship used to feel smaller to me and, in some ways, more solid. When I was younger, a friend was someone I saw at school, someone whose house I had been to, someone whose voice I knew without checking a screen. If I wanted to tell them something, I had to wait until lunch or call their home phone and hope their parents did not pick up. That kind of friendship could be slow and frustrating, but it had weight. Every interaction felt deliberate. You had to make time for each other.

Social media changed that. At first it felt almost miraculous. Friendship was no longer limited by distance, schedules, or shyness. I could keep up with people from old schools, summer programs, family trips, and later from completely different phases of life. Someone I had not seen in years could still show up in my day through a photo, a joke, a birthday post, or a message sent after midnight. Social media made friendship feel ongoing, as if people never had to vanish completely.

There is something lovely about that. I have been able to see the ordinary details of my friends' lives in a way that would have been impossible before: new apartments, bad haircuts, pets, travel photos, engagements, breakups, quiet wins. I have stayed connected to people I might otherwise have lost. Sometimes one small reaction to a story is enough to reopen a conversation. A friendship that might have faded can keep going through those small digital gestures. Social media has made it easier to say, "I'm still here. I still know you."

But it has also changed friendship in ways that unsettle me. It can create a feeling of intimacy without asking much of us. I can know what someone ate, where they went on vacation, and what political opinion they posted without having any real sense of how they are doing. I can feel caught up on someone's life without ever asking a sincere question. In that way, social media can turn friendship into passive observation. We watch each other instead of actually meeting.

It has also blurred the meaning of the word "friend." The number can climb into the hundreds or thousands, but that abundance can hide a different kind of loneliness. Being visible is not the same as being known. Getting likes is not the same as being comforted. Social media encourages performance, and friendship can get tangled up in that performance too. Instead of sharing ourselves, we start curating ourselves, even for people who care about us. The pressure to seem happy, funny, successful, or unbothered can make honesty feel risky.

I do not think social media has ruined friendship. I think it has exposed what friendship can and cannot do. It can help us stay in touch, but it cannot replace presence. It can start conversations, but it cannot make them deep. The friendships that matter most in my life are the ones that hold up both online and off: the people I can send memes to, but also call in a crisis; the people who notice when I go quiet; the people who know the version of me that exists beyond a profile.

Social media made friendship broader, faster, and more constant. What it could not change is how friendship is really built: attention, honesty, time, and care.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It stands on the banks of the Mtkvari River in the eastern part of the country and is Georgia’s political, economic, and cultural center, with a population of more than one million.

Its location between Europe and Asia made it an important center for trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange for much of its history.

The city’s name comes from the Georgian word “tbili,” meaning “warm,” after the area’s natural sulfur hot springs. According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded Tbilisi in the 5th century after discovering the springs while hunting, though archaeological evidence shows that the area was settled earlier. Tbilisi later became the capital of the eastern Georgian kingdom and grew into a major urban center on regional trade routes.

Over the centuries, Tbilisi was contested by Persians, Arabs, Byzantines, Seljuks, Mongols, and Ottomans. In the 19th century, Russian imperial expansion brought the city under the Russian Empire, where it became an important administrative center in the Caucasus. After periods of independence and Soviet rule, Tbilisi became the capital of independent Georgia in 1991 after the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Tbilisi is known for architecture that reflects its long and varied history. The Old Town has narrow streets, traditional wooden balconies, churches, mosques, and bathhouses. Later districts include neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet modernist, and contemporary buildings. Major landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sameba Cathedral, Rustaveli Avenue, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani.

The city is also the main center of education, arts, and science in Georgia. It is home to Tbilisi State University, one of the oldest universities in the Caucasus, along with museums, theaters, galleries, and research institutions. Among its leading cultural institutions are the Georgian National Museum, the Shota Rustaveli Theatre, and the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre.

Tbilisi has a diverse economy built on services, finance, tourism, transportation, and industry. It is also the country’s main transportation hub, with an international airport, railway links, and a metro system. In recent decades, the city has gone through extensive redevelopment and modernization while keeping much of its historic character.

Today, Tbilisi is known for its multicultural heritage, active public life, and distinctive urban landscape. It remains one of the most important cities in the South Caucasus and a symbol of Georgian statehood and identity.

# Library of Alexandria

The Library of Alexandria was one of the largest and most prestigious libraries of the ancient world. It stood in Alexandria, Egypt, and was founded in the early 3rd century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty. It was part of the Mouseion, a research institution dedicated to the Muses. Over time, it came to represent ancient scholarship and, in popular culture, the loss of knowledge through destruction.

## History

The library was probably established during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (r. 305–282 BCE) or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 284–246 BCE). Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian exile, is traditionally said to have advised on its creation, though modern scholars debate how much he was involved. The Ptolemies aimed to collect texts from across the known world. Ancient sources say that ships entering Alexandria's harbor were searched for books, which were copied and sometimes retained, while the owners received the copies.

## Collection and scholarship

Ancient estimates of the library's holdings range from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, but historians generally consider those figures unreliable. The collection included literature, history, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy. Most of the works were in Greek, though some were translations from other languages. Tradition also holds that the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.

The library drew prominent scholars to Alexandria. Euclid is associated with the city and is said to have produced his *Elements* there. Eratosthenes, who served as librarian, calculated the Earth's circumference. Other figures linked to the library include Aristarchus of Samothrace, who edited Homeric texts, and Callimachus, who compiled the *Pinakes*, an early catalog of the collection. Herophilus and Erasistratus advanced the study of anatomy in the city.

## Decline and destruction

The library seems to have declined over time rather than disappearing in a single event. Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE, set during his conflict in Alexandria, damaged part of the city and may have destroyed some books, though the scale is unclear. Under Roman rule, royal funding and patronage declined. Aurelian's campaign in the 270s CE devastated the district that contained the Mouseion. The Serapeum, sometimes described as a daughter library, was destroyed in 391 CE under Bishop Theophilus. Most historians regard the story that the Arab conqueror Amr ibn al-As burned the library in 642 CE as a later legend.

## Modern legacy

In 2002, Egypt opened the Bibliotheca Alexandrina near the ancient site. It is a modern library and cultural center meant to revive the spirit of the original institution.

## See also

- Ptolemaic Kingdom
- Library of Pergamum
- Septuagint

# Plugin system documentation

## Overview

The editor's plugin system lets you add features without changing the core application. Plugins are written in JavaScript and run in an isolated sandbox. They communicate with the editor through a controlled API.

## Installing plugins

Place plugin folders in your user plugin directory:

- Windows: `%APPDATA%\Editor\plugins`
- macOS/Linux: `~/.config/editor/plugins`

You can also open the command palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and run `Plugins: Install from Registry`. To activate a new plugin, restart the editor or run `Plugins: Reload All`.

## Plugin structure

Each plugin needs a folder with at least two files:

```
my-plugin/
├── manifest.json
└── index.js
```

### manifest.json

The manifest describes the plugin:

```json
{
  "name": "word-counter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "permissions": ["editor.read", "ui.statusbar"],
  "activationEvents": ["onStartup"]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `name` | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `version` | Semantic version string |
| `main` | Entry point file |
| `permissions` | APIs the plugin can access |
| `activationEvents` | When the plugin loads |

## Writing a plugin

Your entry file must export an `activate` function. Export `deactivate` if the plugin needs cleanup.

```javascript
exports.activate = function (editor) {
  const item = editor.ui.createStatusItem();

  editor.on("textChanged", () => {
    const text = editor.document.getText();
    item.setText(`Words: ${text.split(/\s+/).length}`);
  });
};

exports.deactivate = function () {
  // Release resources here
};
```

## Core API

- `editor.document`: Read and modify the active file (`getText()`, `insert()`, `replace()`)
- `editor.commands`: Register commands with `registerCommand(id, handler)`
- `editor.ui`: Create status items, menus, and panels
- `editor.on(event, callback)`: Subscribe to events such as `textChanged`, `fileSaved`, and `selectionChanged`
- `editor.settings`: Read user configuration values

## Permissions

Plugins can use only the APIs declared in their manifest. Common permissions include:

- `editor.read`: Read document contents
- `editor.write`: Modify documents
- `ui.statusbar`: Add status bar items
- `fs.read`: Read files in the workspace
- `network`: Make external requests

Users are asked to approve permissions when they install a plugin for the first time.

## Debugging

Open `Help → Toggle Plugin Console` to view `console.log` output and uncaught errors. After making changes, run `Plugins: Reload All` to load the updated plugin.

## Best practices

1. Request only the permissions you need.
2. Use specific activation events instead of `onStartup` so the editor starts faster.
3. Dispose of event listeners in `deactivate`.
4. Avoid blocking operations. Use asynchronous calls for file and network access.

# API caching layer

## Overview

This document proposes a distributed cache for the web API to reduce database load, lower response times, and handle peak traffic more smoothly.

## Problem statement

The API currently queries the primary PostgreSQL database on every request. Profiling shows that 80% of traffic goes to read-only endpoints such as product catalogs, user profiles, and configuration data, and many of those requests return the same results. During peak hours, p95 latency goes above 800 ms and database CPU regularly reaches 85%.

## Goals

- Reduce p95 latency on read endpoints to under 150 ms
- Cut database read load by at least 60%
- Keep staleness under 60 seconds for most resources
- Avoid changes to client-facing API contracts

## Non-goals

- Caching authenticated write operations
- Replacing the database as the source of truth

## Proposed solution

Add Redis as a cache-aside layer between the API servers and the database.

For reads, the API checks Redis with a deterministic key such as `product:v1:{id}`. On a cache hit, it returns the cached value. On a miss, it queries the database, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it.

For writes, the API invalidates the relevant keys after an update or deletion. For list and search results, we will use short TTLs of 30 seconds instead of explicit invalidation because dependency tracking is error-prone.

### Key design

- Version prefixes allow bulk invalidation after schema changes
- Per-user data includes the user ID in the key to prevent leakage

### TTL strategy

| Resource | TTL |
|---|---|
| Configuration | 10 min |
| Product details | 5 min (plus invalidation) |
| Lists/search | 30 sec |

## Risks and mitigations

- Stampedes: When popular keys expire, many requests may hit the database at once. We will use request coalescing and add random jitter of plus or minus 10% to TTLs.
- Stale data: Explicit invalidation on writes and conservative TTLs limit exposure.
- Redis outage: The API will fall back to the database with a circuit breaker and accept degraded performance instead of failing requests.
- Memory growth: Enforce `allkeys-lru` eviction and monitor memory usage.

## Rollout plan

1. Deploy a managed Redis cluster with replication
2. Implement caching behind a feature flag, starting with configuration endpoints
3. Roll out to 10%, then 50%, then 100% of traffic for each endpoint
4. Monitor hit rate, latency, and error rates at each stage

## Success metrics

Target a cache hit rate above 75%, p95 latency under 150 ms, and database CPU below 50% at peak.

## Open questions

- Should we add an in-process L1 cache for extremely hot keys?
- Is a CDN appropriate for public, unauthenticated endpoints?

# Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It lifted off 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. Relative to the Sun, it travels at about 17 kilometers per second, or roughly 61,000 km/h.

## Mission background

The Voyager program took advantage of a rare alignment of the outer planets that happens about once every 175 years. That alignment let spacecraft use gravity assists to visit multiple planets. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory built the probes, which were originally funded for a four-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn.

## Spacecraft design

Voyager 1 had a launch mass of about 825 kilograms. It carries a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna to communicate with the Deep Space Network. Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs, supply power by converting heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Their output drops by several watts each year, so engineers have had to shut down nonessential instruments and heaters over time. The spacecraft also carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated phonograph record with sounds, images, and music meant to represent life and culture on Earth.

## Planetary encounters

Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter on March 5, 1979. During that encounter, it revealed active volcanism on Io, the first volcanic activity observed beyond Earth. It reached Saturn on November 12, 1980, and returned detailed images of the rings and of Titan, Saturn's largest moon, whose thick atmosphere it studied closely. The Titan flyby bent the probe's path out of the ecliptic plane and ended its planetary tour. In 1990, Voyager 1 captured the "Family Portrait" of the Solar System, including the image of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot.

## Interstellar mission

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, where the Sun's solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium. It was the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument recorded a sharp rise in plasma density that confirmed the crossing.

In November 2023, the probe began sending unintelligible data because of a fault in one of its onboard computers. Engineers at JPL traced the problem to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem. In 2024, they restored communication by relocating the affected code, despite the spacecraft being more than 24 billion kilometers away.

## Future

Voyager 1 still transmits data on magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect the RTGs to power at least one instrument into the mid-2020s, and possibly longer. Built with 1977-era technology, the probe will eventually drift through the Milky Way and pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in roughly 40,000 years.

## See also

- Voyager 2
- Voyager program
- Pioneer 10
- Golden Record

# Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It lifted off 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. Relative to the Sun, it travels at about 17 kilometers per second, or roughly 61,000 km/h.

## Mission background

The Voyager program took advantage of a rare alignment of the outer planets that happens about once every 175 years. That alignment let spacecraft use gravity assists to visit multiple planets. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory built the probes, which were originally funded for a four-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn.

## Spacecraft design

Voyager 1 had a launch mass of about 825 kilograms. It carries a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna to communicate with the Deep Space Network. Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs, supply power by converting heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Their output drops by several watts each year, so engineers have had to shut down nonessential instruments and heaters over time. The spacecraft also carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated phonograph record with sounds, images, and music meant to represent life and culture on Earth.

## Planetary encounters

Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter on March 5, 1979. During that encounter, it revealed active volcanism on Io, the first volcanic activity observed beyond Earth. It reached Saturn on November 12, 1980, and returned detailed images of the rings and of Titan, Saturn's largest moon, whose thick atmosphere it studied closely. The Titan flyby bent the probe's path out of the ecliptic plane and ended its planetary tour. In 1990, Voyager 1 captured the "Family Portrait" of the Solar System, including the image of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot.

## Interstellar mission

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, where the Sun's solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium. It was the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument recorded a sharp rise in plasma density that confirmed the crossing.

In November 2023, the probe began sending unintelligible data because of a fault in one of its onboard computers. Engineers at JPL traced the problem to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem. In 2024, they restored communication by relocating the affected code, despite the spacecraft being more than 24 billion kilometers away.

## Future

Voyager 1 still transmits data on magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect the RTGs to power at least one instrument into the mid-2020s, and possibly longer. Built with 1977-era technology, the probe will eventually drift through the Milky Way and pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in roughly 40,000 years.

## See also

- Voyager 2
- Voyager program
- Pioneer 10
- Golden Record

When I was nine, my family moved to a new town in the middle of winter, and for weeks I didn't know anyone. My mother worked two jobs. My father was still in our old city, finishing out a lease. The apartment was small and quiet, and the afternoons felt endless. One day I followed a stranger's dog down the street and wound up at the public library.

I didn't know it then, but I'd found the one place in town that wanted nothing from me.

That's what stays with me now. As an adult, I've learned how unusual that is. Most places expect something in return for letting you be there. Coffee shops want you to buy a latte. Malls want a receipt. Even parks come with rules and closing hours. The library says: come in, sit down, stay as long as you want. It may be the last truly free room in American life, and I think we overlook it because it asks so little of us.

People say libraries are obsolete, that everything is online now. That misses the point. Yes, a library lends books, and that alone still feels a little miraculous: a shared shelf where one copy of a novel might pass through fifty hands. But spend an afternoon in a library and you'll see how much else happens there. A man in a worn jacket fills out a job application on a public computer while a librarian helps him attach his résumé. A teenager does homework because there's no internet at home. A toddler learns to sit still through a story. Someone gets help with tax forms. Someone else practices English. Someone else is simply warm, out of the cold, and safe for a few hours.

These people are not customers. They are citizens, and the library treats them that way.

There's something radical in the library's basic promise: access to knowledge should not depend on what you can pay. It's an old idea, but it feels especially necessary now. We live in a time when information is everywhere and more of it sits behind paywalls, while algorithms decide what rises to the surface. The library offers something different. Its shelves are put together by people trained to help you find what is true, not what will keep you scrolling. A librarian will answer your question without tracking you, selling your data, or steering you toward an ad.

That winter, I worked my way through the children's section, then the adult section, then whatever a kind librarian slid across the desk with a raised eyebrow and a "Try this." I read about places I'd never see and lives nothing like mine. After a while, I stopped feeling like the new kid. I felt like I belonged to something larger.

I still carry a library card, and it remains one of my most valued possessions. It reminds me of the bargain we made with one another: that we would pool our resources so everyone, whatever their circumstances, could reach a larger world.

That bargain still holds. It's worth keeping.

A major European museum has returned a collection of looted artifacts to Nigeria, in a move many see as an important step in confronting the legacy of colonial plunder.

At a ceremony on Tuesday, the museum formally handed over 27 objects to Nigerian officials, including ceremonial sculptures, carved ivory pieces, and bronze plaques taken during a 19th-century military expedition. The artifacts had been kept in the museum’s African collections for more than a century and are expected to go on display in Lagos after conservation work is completed.

Museum director Elise Hartmann called the return “a moral responsibility and an institutional reckoning.”

“These objects were acquired in circumstances that were deeply unjust,” Hartmann said. “They are part of a living cultural heritage. Returning them is the right thing to do.”

The repatriation follows years of pressure from Nigerian officials, scholars, and activists, who have argued that artifacts seized during colonial campaigns should be returned to the communities they were taken from. Recent provenance research by the museum found that the objects were removed during a British punitive raid in 1897 and later sold through European art markets before entering the museum’s collection.

Nigeria’s Minister of Culture, Amina Bello, welcomed the return and called it “an important act of justice, dignity, and historical acknowledgment.”

“For generations, these treasures were admired abroad while the people to whom they belong were denied access to them,” Bello said. “Their return does not erase the past, but it helps us confront it honestly and begin to repair the damage.”

The decision comes as more museums in Europe and North America revisit the origins of objects acquired during the colonial period. In recent years, several institutions have announced the return of bronzes, sacred objects, and human remains after evidence showed they had been taken through violence, coercion, or theft.

The issue is still contentious. Some critics say museums serve an international public and should keep major collections while sharing them through loans and partnerships. Others argue that full repatriation is necessary to address long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Experts say the latest return could prompt similar action elsewhere. “This is not just about one museum or one set of objects,” said art historian Daniel Okoye. “It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely.”

The museum said it will continue reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection and is in discussions with other countries about possible returns.

For many observers, Tuesday’s handover was more than a transfer of property. It was a public acknowledgment that these historical wounds can no longer be kept behind glass.

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered device, often described as the earliest known analog computer. It was built to calculate and display astronomical events, including the positions of the Sun and Moon, lunar phases, eclipse cycles, and possibly the movements of some planets. Most scholars date it to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE.

It was found in 1901 in a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. The recovered pieces were heavily corroded bronze fragments, and at first they drew little notice. Their complexity only became clear later, when researchers found finely cut gears inside them. Modern imaging, especially X-ray computed tomography, has since revealed much of the mechanism’s internal structure and inscriptions.

The device sat inside a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its front face had circular dials with pointers showing astronomical information, probably including the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar. A hand crank likely drove a system of more than 30 bronze gears. Those gears turned rotational motion into mathematical relationships that matched celestial cycles. The mechanism also modeled the Moon’s uneven motion with unusual sophistication, using a pin-and-slot system to simulate changes in lunar speed in line with ancient Greek astronomical theory.

On the back were spiral dials for tracking longer cycles. One showed the Metonic cycle of 19 years, which brings lunar months into line with the solar year. Another tracked the Saros cycle, which was used to predict eclipses. A smaller dial seems to have marked the Exeligmos, a longer eclipse cycle that improved prediction. Inscriptions on the device worked like an operating guide, explaining the dials and displays.

The Antikythera mechanism points to a level of technical skill that historians did not once expect from the Hellenistic world. Its precise gearing suggests a well-developed tradition of instrument-making, even though no other surviving device from antiquity matches its complexity. Scholars have connected it to Greek scientific traditions associated with figures such as Hipparchus, Posidonius, and Archimedes, though its exact origin and maker are still unknown.

The mechanism changed how modern scholars understand ancient science and technology. It shows that Greek craftsmen and astronomers could turn advanced mathematical knowledge into intricate mechanical form. Often called centuries ahead of its time, the Antikythera mechanism remains one of the most famous archaeological discoveries in the history of science.

The first time I stood in a city center without cars, I didn't notice that they were gone. I noticed the sounds instead: a busker with an out-of-tune accordion, a toddler shrieking at a pigeon, two old men arguing over a chessboard. It took me a full minute to register what was missing: that low, constant growl I had always mistaken for silence.

This was in a mid-sized European city I visited mostly to get away from my own. At home, I drive everywhere. I'm not proud of that, but it's true. My downtown is something I put up with: circling for parking, paying too much for it, then walking half a mile past gray garages. So when people talk about banning cars from city centers, I still feel my guard go up. What about groceries? What about my mother, who can't walk far? What about the plumber, the ambulance, the delivery driver?

Those are fair questions, and the best car-free centers answer them. Ambulances and fire trucks still get through. Residents with disabilities get permits and drop-off access. Deliveries happen in early-morning windows. Done well, a ban works more like a filter than a wall. It means the busiest and most valuable part of a city isn't built around the least efficient way to move people through it.

Because it is inefficient. One lane of car traffic moves maybe 2,000 people an hour. Give that same width to a tram or a crowd of pedestrians and it carries far more. We give huge amounts of prime space to parked cars, then act surprised when rents rise and public space disappears.

Even so, I can't give a simple yes. I've seen cities impose bans without offering much else: no reliable buses, no protected bike lanes, no affordable option for people who still need to get in. In those places, a ban doesn't produce some bustling plaza. It hits the shift worker coming from the outskirts at midnight, after the trains stop running. When cities ban first and build later, the people taking the risk are usually the ones with the least margin.

So my view is conditional, but it's firm. Cities should move toward car-free centers, and they should earn that change by building the alternatives first, or at least at the same time. Make the train faster than driving. Make the bike lane feel safe to an eleven-year-old. Then close the street, and most people won't put up much of a fight.

What changed my mind wasn't the numbers. It was that square at dusk, when the chess players packed up and families drifted in, and kids wove between café tables without a parent gripping their shoulder. No one was in a rush. No one looked at risk. I realized I'd never seen a city center act like a living room before.

I still drive at home. But I've started parking on the edge of downtown and walking the rest of the way. At first it felt like giving something up. Now it feels like practice for something better: a city where the center belongs to the people who are actually in it.

# Artemisia Gentileschi

Artemisia Gentileschi (8 July 1593 to about 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter and one of the most accomplished artists of her generation. She worked in the tradition of Caravaggio and became known for dramatic compositions, a naturalistic style, and forceful depictions of women from myth, scripture, and history. She was the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence.

## Early life

Artemisia was born in Rome, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi and Prudentia Montone. Her mother died when she was about twelve. She trained in her father's workshop, where she learned drawing, color mixing, and painting. Because women were barred from formal academies, most of her education took place in the studio. Her earliest signed work, Susanna and the Elders (1610), already shows unusual skill for a seventeen-year-old.

## Trial of Agostino Tassi

In 1611, Artemisia was raped by Agostino Tassi, a painter and colleague of her father who had been hired to teach her perspective. Orazio brought charges the next year, and the trial lasted seven months. During the proceedings, Artemisia was reportedly examined under torture with thumbscrews to test her testimony. Tassi was convicted, but his sentence of exile from Rome was only briefly enforced. The surviving trial transcripts are a rare record of a woman's testimony from this period.

## Career

Soon after the trial, Artemisia married the Florentine artist Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence. She succeeded there, gained the patronage of Cosimo II de' Medici, and became friends with Galileo Galilei. In 1616 she was admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Paintings from this period include Judith Slaying Holofernes (c. 1614 to 1620) and Self-Portrait as a Lute Player.

Financial problems and debt took her back to Rome in the 1620s, and she later worked in Venice and Naples. In 1638 she joined her father at the court of Charles I in England. After Orazio's death in 1639, she completed some of his commissions. She spent much of her later career in Naples, where she worked with other painters and received major commissions.

## Style and themes

Gentileschi's paintings are marked by strong chiaroscuro, vivid color, and emotional intensity. She often painted figures such as Judith, Susanna, Esther, Bathsheba, and Cleopatra. Her women are physically strong and psychologically complex, unlike the more passive figures often painted by her male contemporaries.

## Legacy

After her death, Gentileschi was largely overlooked for centuries. In the 20th century, art historians, especially feminist scholars, brought renewed attention to her work and reassessed its importance. Her life and art later inspired books, plays, and films, and major exhibitions, including one at the National Gallery in London in 2020, helped establish her as a leading Baroque painter.

# Migration guide: config format v1 to v2

Version 2 changes the config layout, tightens type checking, and uses clearer field names. This guide covers the main changes and how to update an existing v1 file.

## Breaking changes

1. Top-level keys are now grouped into sections.
2. Some field names have changed.
3. Boolean and numeric values must use proper YAML or JSON types, not strings.
4. Environment-specific overrides now live under an `environments` block.
5. Deprecated v1 fields are no longer supported.

## Key changes

### 1. Top-level structure

In v1, most settings were defined at the root level. In v2, they are grouped under these sections:

- `server`
- `logging`
- `auth`
- `environments`

### 2. Renamed fields

Common renames:

- `host` → `server.host`
- `port` → `server.port`
- `logLevel` → `logging.level`
- `logFile` → `logging.file`
- `enableAuth` → `auth.enabled`

### 3. Strict value types

In v1, values like `"true"` and `"8080"` were often accepted as strings. In v2, use native types instead:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

v1 often used flat keys like `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2, put those values under `environments`:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed fields

These v1 fields are not supported in v2:

- `timeoutMs` — replaced by `server.timeout` in seconds
- `authModeLegacy` — removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug` — replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before deployment.
- Update any automation that still reads the old field names.
- Check for quoted booleans and numbers, since they now fail validation.
- Migrate in stages and test in a staging environment first.

## Final checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the correct sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

After these changes, the configuration will be compatible with v2.

In v1, values like `"true"` and `"8080"` were often accepted as strings. In v2, use native types instead:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

v1 often used flat keys like `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2, put those values under `environments`:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed fields

These v1 fields are not supported in v2:

- `timeoutMs` — replaced by `server.timeout` in seconds
- `authModeLegacy` — removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug` — replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before deployment.
- Update any automation that still reads the old field names.
- Check for quoted booleans and numbers, since they now fail validation.
- Migrate in stages and test in a staging environment first.

## Final checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the correct sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

After these changes, the configuration will be compatible with v2.

# photodate

`photodate` renames your photos based on when they were taken. It reads EXIF metadata and uses a consistent, sortable format like `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Read the original capture date from EXIF data
- Fall back to the file's modified time if EXIF is missing
- Use custom filename templates
- Preview changes with dry-run mode
- Handle duplicate timestamps automatically
- Undo the most recent run
- Work with JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

With pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

Requires Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can be one or more files or directories.

### Quick start

Preview changes:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Rename files:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Include subfolders:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Show planned renames without changing anything |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | Process directories recursively |
| `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE` | Filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`) |
| `--fallback [mtime\|skip]` | What to do when EXIF is missing (default: `mtime`) |
| `--prefix TEXT` | Add a prefix to every filename |
| `--lowercase-ext` | Convert file extensions to lowercase |
| `--undo` | Revert the last run |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print every rename |

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%Y` | Four-digit year |
| `%m` | Month (01–12) |
| `%d` | Day of month |
| `%H` `%M` `%S` | Hour, minute, second |

## Duplicate timestamps

Burst shots often share the same timestamp. If two files would get the same name, `photodate` adds a counter:

```
2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_2.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_3.jpg
```

It never overwrites existing files.

## Undo

Each run writes a log to `~/.photodate/last_run.json`. To revert the last run:

```bash
photodate --undo
```

Only the most recent run can be undone.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before submitting changes.

## License

MIT

A regional museum in northern England formally returned 27 artifacts to Nigeria on Tuesday, ending a decade of negotiations over objects taken during a colonial military expedition in 1897.

At a ceremony in Hartwell, the Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments. Diplomats, museum staff, and members of the Edo diaspora attended. The collection includes brass plaques, carved ivory pieces, and a ceremonial staff from the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

"These are not simply objects," said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, who led the Nigerian delegation. "They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes."

British forces took the artifacts in 1897 when they attacked Benin City and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many were later sold at auction or dispersed among private collectors and institutions in Europe and North America. The Hartwell museum acquired its pieces in 1934 through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision followed extensive provenance research that confirmed the objects' origins beyond reasonable doubt. "We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," Marsh said. "Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

The return comes as Western museums face growing pressure to confront colonial-era acquisitions. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States, and Scotland have returned parts of their Benin collections. The British Museum, which holds a much larger collection, continues to face calls for restitution.

Not everyone supports the returns. Some curators say so-called universal museums give international audiences access to many cultures in one place. Others have questioned whether returned works can be properly conserved. Supporters of restitution point to Nigeria's plans for the Edo Museum of West African Art, a new facility designed by architect David Adjaye to house returned works.

For Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent who attended the ceremony, the handover felt personal. "My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes," he said. "I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime."

The artifacts will be flown to Lagos next week and then taken to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

Boredom gets a worse reputation than it deserves. We talk about it like a small curse, something to avoid almost as urgently as hunger or loneliness. A boring class, a boring conversation, a boring afternoon all feel like failures, as if life is supposed to keep us entertained at all times. I used to think that too. If I was waiting in line, sitting on a bus, or lying there with nothing immediate to do, I would reach for my phone without even thinking. I treated every empty patch in the day like something that needed fixing. It took me a while to see that boredom is not always just emptiness. Sometimes it opens into something else.

I knew this better as a child than I do now. Summer afternoons could feel endless. The heat was too heavy to run around outside, there was nothing good on TV, and my friends were gone. At first, those hours felt unbearable. I would wander from room to room and announce to anyone nearby that there was "nothing to do." Then, after I had worn out the complaint, something usually shifted. Blankets turned into forts. Notebooks became newspapers for imaginary cities. A box of mismatched buttons became treasure. I had to get through boredom before my imagination started moving.

That never really changed. Adult life just makes it easier to miss. There is always some escape nearby, usually glowing in your hand. The second a task gets repetitive or a silence lasts a little too long, distraction is right there. But constant stimulation leaves me feeling strangely thinned out, as if my attention has been split into too many pieces to rest anywhere. Boredom does the opposite. It slows things down long enough for thoughts I have been avoiding, or simply been too busy to hear, to come up.

Some of my clearest ideas have shown up in boring moments: folding laundry, walking the same route again, sitting through the first dull minutes of a delayed train. In those moments, my mind wanders, and that is not the same as wasting time. Usually it is where reflection starts. Boredom removes the sense of urgency and makes room for a different kind of attention, less efficient maybe, but wider. It gives memory, curiosity, and even discomfort a chance to speak. Without it, I think I would understand much less about what I actually think.

Boredom has a moral side too. It forces us to face the fact that not every moment exists to amuse us. The world does not owe us novelty on demand. Learning to tolerate tedium, to sit in a waiting room, to stay with a quiet pause, to let an afternoon pass without demanding instant gratification, is a kind of patience. It teaches humility. A meaningful life is not made only of exciting scenes. It is also made of ordinary stretches that ask for endurance, attention, and a little invention.

I still dislike being bored. I still reach for distraction more often than I want to. But I do not see boredom as a void that needs to be filled as fast as possible anymore. I see it as a necessary pause, a stretch of unfilled time in which something quieter can appear. In a culture that fears silence and chases stimulation, boredom may be one of the few places left where the mind can hear itself think.

# Contributing guide

Thanks for contributing to our open-source documentation site. You can help in lots of ways, from fixing a typo to adding new content or reorganizing a section.

## Ways to contribute

You can help by:

- fixing spelling, grammar, or formatting issues
- clarifying existing explanations
- adding examples, tutorials, or reference material
- reporting outdated or incorrect information
- improving accessibility and readability
- suggesting better navigation or organization

If you are not sure whether something fits, open an issue first.

## Before you start

Before you begin:

- read the existing documentation style and structure
- search open issues and pull requests to avoid duplicate work
- check whether there is already a discussion about the change you want to make

For larger changes, open an issue before you start writing. It helps set expectations and can save time.

## Getting started

1. Fork the repository.
2. Create a new branch for your changes.
3. Make your edits.
4. Preview the site locally, if you can.
5. Commit your changes with a clear message.
6. Open a pull request.

Use descriptive branch names such as `fix-installation-typo` or `add-api-auth-guide`.

## Writing guidelines

To keep the documentation consistent:

- write in clear, direct language
- use short paragraphs and descriptive headings
- prefer examples to abstract explanations
- keep terminology consistent across pages
- link to related pages when helpful
- avoid unnecessary jargon

If you add technical content, make sure examples are accurate and easy to follow. If you include a command or code snippet, test it when possible.

## Style and formatting

Please follow the project's formatting conventions, including:

- Markdown structure and heading levels
- code block formatting with language tags
- file naming patterns
- internal linking style

If the repository includes linting or formatting tools, run them before submitting your pull request.

## Pull request expectations

A good pull request should:

- clearly explain what changed
- explain why the change is needed
- stay focused on a single topic when possible
- include screenshots or previews for visual changes, if relevant

Be open to feedback. Reviews are a normal part of the process, and collaboration usually leads to a better result.

## Reporting issues

If you find a problem but do not want to submit a fix, open an issue and include:

- a clear title
- a link to the affected page
- a description of the problem
- a suggestion, if you have one

## Code of conduct

Please be respectful and constructive in all interactions. We want the project to be welcoming to contributors at all experience levels.

## Thank you

Every contribution helps make the documentation better. We appreciate your time, effort, and ideas.

When people talk about the decline of letter writing, they usually begin with nostalgia: the romance of envelopes, the elegance of stamps, the little jolt of recognizing a familiar hand before you read a word. All of that is real. But when we stop writing letters, we lose more than an old ritual. We lose a way of thinking and feeling, and a way of being present to one another.

A letter asks something different of us than a text or an email. It asks us to sit still long enough to find out what we actually want to say. In most modern communication, speed is the point. We reply quickly, revise invisibly, send half-formed thoughts, and fill silence before it has time to deepen. A letter moves at the pace of reflection. Because it takes time to write, seal, send, and receive, it invites a kind of honesty that is less impulsive and more deliberate. You do not usually spend a letter on what you had for lunch or some passing irritation. You gather yourself. You shape experience into language. Often, in the process, you come to understand your own mind a little better.

One of the quietest losses, I think, is that when we stop writing letters, we lose a private workshop for the self. A letter is not quite conversation and not quite diary. It lives in the intimate space between them. It is personal, but directed outward. You reveal yourself not into the void, but to a particular person. That matters. In letters, we often become slightly better versions of ourselves: more thoughtful, more generous, more willing to explain what we mean. Writing to someone we love can refine not only our words, but our character.

Letters also preserve feeling in a way instant messages rarely do. A text can say “I miss you,” but a letter carries physical evidence of having been made by someone’s hands. The pressure of the pen, the slant of the lines, the crossed-out words, the note in the margin added as an afterthought: these are not decorative details. They are traces of a living moment. A letter is language, but it is also an object. It travels through weather and distance. It can be folded into a drawer, opened again years later, and return a lost version of a person to us. To hold an old letter is to encounter not only what someone felt, but how they moved through time.

When we stop writing letters, we also lose patience with absence. Letters teach us to wait. That waiting is not empty. It enlarges affection. It gives longing room to ripen into attention. In an age when we can reach anyone instantly, we often expect access instead of presence. We mistake constant contact for closeness. But closeness does not always grow from frequency. Sometimes it grows from concentration, from choosing words carefully, from speaking across silence instead of erasing it.

I do not think we need to reject newer forms of communication to grieve what letters gave us. Texts are useful, emails are efficient, calls are immediate. But letters offered something these forms rarely do: a lasting record of thought shaped by time and care. When we stop writing letters, we lose not only an art, but a human tempo. We lose one of the few ways of communicating that asks us to slow down enough to mean what we say.

Migrating from v1 to v2 mostly comes down to a few format changes in your config files. This guide shows what changed and how to update YAML files.

## Summary of changes

| Area | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Version field | Optional | Required (`version: 2`) |
| Server settings | Flat keys | Nested under `server` |
| Timeouts | Integers (seconds) | Duration strings (`"30s"`) |
| Environment variables | `$VAR` | `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` |
| Booleans | `yes`/`no` accepted | `true`/`false` only |
| `log_file` | Supported | Removed; use `logging.output` |

## Step 1: Add the version field

Add this to the top of every file. v2 parsers reject files that do not include it.

```yaml
version: 2
```

## Step 2: Nest server settings

The `host`, `port`, and `timeout` keys now belong under `server`.

v1

```yaml
host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8080
timeout: 30
```

v2

```yaml
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  timeout: "30s"
```

## Step 3: Convert timeouts to durations

All time values now have to be strings with a unit: `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`. Bare integers now fail validation. In v1 they were treated as seconds, which was easy to misread.

## Step 4: Update environment variable syntax

Change `$DB_PASSWORD` to `${DB_PASSWORD}`. You can also add a fallback value:

```yaml
database:
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
```

Escape literal dollar signs as `$$`.

## Step 5: Replace deprecated options

`log_file` is gone in v2. Use the `logging` block instead.

v1

```yaml
log_file: /var/log/app.log
```

v2

```yaml
logging:
  output: /var/log/app.log
  level: info
```

# Atacama Desert

The Atacama Desert (Spanish: *Desierto de Atacama*) is a desert plateau on the Pacific coast of western South America. It stretches about 1,600 km (1,000 mi), mostly across northern Chile. It is often described as the driest non-polar desert in the world and one of the oldest continuously arid regions on Earth.

## Geography

The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes, extending from the southern border of Peru to around La Serena in Chile. It covers about 105,000 km² (41,000 sq mi), though broader definitions that include nearby arid areas produce a larger figure. The landscape includes salt flats (*salares*), sand dunes, rocky plains, and volcanic peaks. The Salar de Atacama, the largest salt flat in Chile, lies in the eastern part of the region.

## Climate

The Atacama's extreme dryness comes from several factors. The Andes block moisture from the Amazon Basin to the east, while the cold Humboldt Current and a persistent subtropical high-pressure system limit rainfall from the Pacific. Some weather stations in the interior have never recorded rain, and many areas receive less than 15 mm (0.6 in) of precipitation a year. Evidence suggests that parts of the desert have remained hyperarid for millions of years.

Even so, coastal areas often experience a persistent fog called *camanchaca*, which provides moisture for some plant and animal life.

## Ecology

Vegetation is sparse, but the desert still supports specialized life, including cacti, lichens, and hardy shrubs. In rare years of heavy rain, often linked to El Niño, parts of the desert bloom in the phenomenon known as *desierto florido* ("flowering desert"). Animals in the region include vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and many reptiles and insects. Researchers have also studied microbial life in the soil, which is sometimes compared to that of Mars.

## History and economy

Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures, lived in the region for thousands of years. In the 19th century, the desert became economically important for its nitrate (saltpeter) and guano deposits, both important for fertilizer production. Control of these resources helped drive the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), in which Chile gained territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Today, mining dominates the economy, especially copper and lithium. The Chuquicamata mine is one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

The desert's high altitude, dry air, and low light pollution make it one of the best places in the world for astronomical observation. Major facilities include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, home to the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Popular destinations include San Pedro de Atacama, Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and several high-altitude lagoons.

I didn’t mean to become someone who walks everywhere. It started because my car was in the shop for a week, and taking the bus to work meant a transfer and another forty minutes. So one gray Tuesday I left the house on foot, annoyed, assuming I’d sort something out along the way.

By about mile three, I realized I hadn’t been alone with my own thoughts in years.

Walking creates a strange kind of attention. It’s slow enough that your mind can wander, but your body still has something to do. Problems I’d been carrying for weeks started to loosen on their own. I’d turn a corner and suddenly know how to write the difficult email, or realize I was angry at my brother for the wrong reason. Nietzsche said that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. I can’t say much for the great ones, but the useful ones do seem to show up there.

When the car came back, I kept walking. Mostly in the mornings, before the day started asking things of me. I got to know my neighborhood the way you know a person, not a map. There was the man watering his tomatoes in a faded bathrobe, lifting one finger in greeting like a conductor cueing a single violin. There was the corner where the smell of baking bread drifted out of a vent at exactly 6:40. There was a persimmon tree I passed a hundred times before I noticed it was heavy with fruit, bright as lanterns against the bare branches. I started wondering how much else I’d spent years driving past.

The habit has its own quiet discipline. Some days it rains and I go anyway, and those are often the best walks: the streets rinsed clean and empty, my footsteps the only thing keeping time. Some days I’m tired or sad and the walk doesn’t fix anything, but it lets me carry the sadness at a pace I can manage. Sorrow, I’ve found, is easier to bear at three miles an hour.

I’ve also grown to love the arithmetic of it. A mile is about two thousand steps. A good walk is a few thousand more. None of those steps feels important by itself, and that’s part of why walking matters. No one applauds a single step. Still, they add up, like pennies in a jar, into something solid: a year of mornings, a stronger body, a mind with a little less clutter.

I think a lot now about how much of modern life is built to save us effort and, along with it, experience. Walking asks for your time. In return, it gives back things you may not realize you’ve been missing: the feel of a place, the rhythm of your breathing, the small peace of moving exactly as fast as you can.

Tomorrow morning I’ll lace up my shoes again. I have no idea what I’ll think about, which is exactly why I’ll go.

# Battle of Hastings

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy, and an English army led by the Anglo-Saxon king Harold Godwinson. It took place about 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, near the present-day town of Battle in East Sussex. William won decisively, and the battle began the Norman Conquest of England.

## Background

In January 1066, King Edward the Confessor died without children, which set off a succession crisis. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost at once. William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support that claim. At the same time, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also claimed the throne and invaded northern England in September 1066.

Harold marched north and defeated Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. A few days later, on 28 September, William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast. Harold then rushed his army south, covering roughly 250 miles in about two weeks.

## Battle

Harold's forces took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill and formed a shield wall along the ridge. The English army was made up mostly of infantry, including elite housecarls and the more lightly equipped fyrd. William's army included infantry, archers, crossbowmen, and a large cavalry force.

The fighting began in the morning. Norman archers fired uphill, but they had little effect. Infantry and cavalry attacks followed and failed to break the shield wall. At one point, a rumour spread that William had been killed, and he is said to have lifted his helmet to show that he was still alive. Some Norman troops fell back, and some English soldiers chased them downhill, where the Normans turned and cut them down. Historians still debate whether these retreats were deliberate.

As the day went on, the English line weakened. Harold was killed late in the battle. Tradition says he was struck in the eye by an arrow, as shown in the Bayeux Tapestry, but that remains disputed. With their king dead, the English forces broke and fled.

## Aftermath

William went on to secure his position, received the submission of English leaders, and was crowned King of England on 25 December 1066 at Westminster Abbey. He later founded Battle Abbey on the site of the battle. The conquest changed English society, language, law, and landholding.

## See also

- Norman Conquest
- Bayeux Tapestry
- Battle of Stamford Bridge

Public-transit workers went on strike Tuesday, disrupting commutes across the city and shutting down most bus, subway, and tram service.

The walkout began shortly after midnight, after weeks of failed contract talks between the Transit Workers Union and the Metropolitan Transit Authority. Union leaders say workers want higher wages, stronger job protections, and better staffing. They argue that employees have been under growing pressure for years as living costs rise and labor shortages continue.

"This strike is a last resort," union president Maria Delgado said at an early morning rally outside the transit authority's headquarters. "Our members keep this city moving every day, but they are being asked to do more with less. We need a contract that reflects the value of their work and guarantees safe, reliable service for the public."

Transit officials said they were disappointed by the walkout and warned that a strike lasting several days could hurt the city's economy. In a statement, the authority said it had offered a "fair and responsible" contract package with pay increases and protected benefits, but said the union's demands would put too much strain on an already tight budget.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement as quickly as possible," said transit authority chief executive Daniel Mercer. "We urge union leadership to return to the bargaining table so we can restore service for the millions who depend on public transportation."

By dawn, commuters were crowding rideshare pickup zones, squeezing onto limited regional rail service, and lining up at bike-share stations. Downtown streets grew heavily congested as more residents turned to cars, taxis, and carpools to get to work. Several schools reported higher-than-usual absentee rates, and some businesses said employees were arriving late or working remotely when they could.

City officials urged residents to avoid nonessential travel and announced temporary steps to ease congestion, including expanded bike lanes, more traffic officers at major intersections, and added commuter-rail capacity. The mayor's office said it was monitoring the situation and pushing both sides to resume talks with help from a state-appointed mediator.

For many riders, the strike was a reminder of how much the city depends on public transit. "I understand why workers are upset, but this is chaos," said commuter Jasmine Lee, who spent nearly two hours trying to reach her office. "So many people rely on these trains and buses. I just hope they settle this soon."

Negotiations were expected to continue Tuesday afternoon, though neither side said how close they were to a deal. Until then, residents are preparing for more disruption and another uncertain commute.

Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter and one of the most important artists of the seventeenth century. She was one of the first women to build a successful professional career in a field dominated by men, and she is best known for her paintings of biblical and mythological heroines.

Born in Rome, Artemisia was the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, who gave her her earliest training. Her work was deeply shaped by Caravaggio, especially his dramatic light and shadow, emotional intensity, and naturalism. Even with the limits placed on women’s artistic education at the time, she showed unusual skill early on. One of her earliest known works, Susanna and the Elders (1610), already shows her ability to depict psychological tension and female experience with unusual force.

In 1612, Agostino Tassi, a painter, was tried for raping her. During the trial, Artemisia was subjected to public scrutiny and torture to test her testimony, and the case has played a large role in modern readings of her life and art. Soon after, she married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where her career grew. In 1616, she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno, a mark of her professional standing.

During her years in Florence, and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples, Artemisia painted many of her best-known works, including Judith Slaying Holofernes, Judith and Her Maidservant, Lucretia, and Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting. Her paintings often focus on women from history, scripture, and legend at moments of crisis, courage, or revenge. Subjects like these were common in Baroque art, but Artemisia’s versions are often praised for their intensity, dignity, and emotional complexity.

She also worked for elite patrons in Italy and elsewhere. She spent time in Naples, which became a main center of her later career, and probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of Charles I of England. She may have worked on court commissions there before returning to Naples.

For many years after her death, Artemisia Gentileschi was overshadowed by male contemporaries and often remembered mainly through her biography. Since the twentieth century, her reputation has risen sharply. Scholars have stressed both her technical skill and her originality within Baroque painting. She is now recognized as both a pioneering woman artist and a major painter of her time.

# VoltHaus recalls 42,000 home batteries over overheating risk

Austin-based startup says it has received 31 reports of overheating, including 6 small fires; no injuries reported

AUSTIN, Texas, VoltHaus said Tuesday that it is voluntarily recalling about 42,000 of its HearthCell 10 home battery units after finding a defect that can cause overheating and, in rare cases, fire.

The recall applies to units made between March 2022 and August 2023 and sold in the United States and Canada. The company said it has received 31 reports of overheating worldwide, including six cases in which a unit smoldered or caught fire. No injuries have been reported, though two homeowners said the incidents caused minor damage to garage walls.

VoltHaus said the issue comes from a flaw in a batch of internal wiring connectors supplied by a third-party manufacturer. Under some conditions, including repeated rapid charging in high temperatures, the connectors can degrade and create resistance that produces excess heat.

"Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here," said Dana Okafor, VoltHaus co-founder and chief executive, in a statement. "We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost."

The HearthCell 10 sells for about $8,900 installed and stores solar energy for use at night or during power outages. VoltHaus says it has sold about 60,000 units since launching in 2021, so the recall affects a large share of the batteries it has installed.

Customers can check whether their unit is affected by entering the serial number on the label on the right side of the unit at the company's recall website. VoltHaus is advising affected owners to switch the battery to "limited mode" in its mobile app, which caps charging speed and reduces heat buildup until a technician can make the repair. Owners who cannot access the app are urged to call the company's dedicated hotline.

The company said technicians will replace the connectors in a repair that takes about two hours. Repairs are expected to start next week, with priority for homes where the batteries are installed in attached garages or living spaces.

Analysts say the recall could put pressure on the young company's finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been preparing for a public offering. "A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational," said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. "How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself."

A spokesperson for the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said the agency is reviewing the recall.

"Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here," said Dana Okafor, VoltHaus co-founder and chief executive, in a statement. "We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost."

The HearthCell 10 sells for about $8,900 installed and stores solar energy for use at night or during power outages. VoltHaus says it has sold about 60,000 units since launching in 2021, so the recall affects a large share of the batteries it has installed.

Customers can check whether their unit is affected by entering the serial number on the label on the right side of the unit at the company's recall website. VoltHaus is advising affected owners to switch the battery to "limited mode" in its mobile app, which caps charging speed and reduces heat buildup until a technician can make the repair. Owners who cannot access the app are urged to call the company's dedicated hotline.

The company said technicians will replace the connectors in a repair that takes about two hours. Repairs are expected to start next week, with priority for homes where the batteries are installed in attached garages or living spaces.

Analysts say the recall could put pressure on the young company's finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been preparing for a public offering. "A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational," said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. "How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself."

A spokesperson for the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said the agency is reviewing the recall.
